docs.title: InjectQ Documentation
docs.text:
InjectQ is a type-friendly dependency injection library for Python. It supports sync and async code, scopes, modules, and FastAPI, FastMCP and Taskiq integrations.

Using an AI coding agent?

Give it skill.md: one file with the recommended approach, API, pitfalls and limitations. Rendered page: AI Agent Skill.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ, inject, singleton

container = InjectQ.get_instance()
container[str] = "Hello from InjectQ"   # UserService needs a str

@singleton
class UserService:
    def __init__(self, message: str):
        self.message = message

    def greet(self) -> str:
        return f"Service says: {self.message}"

@inject
def main(service: UserService) -> None:
    print(service.greet())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Dict-like API, bind() methods, @inject and Inject[T]
  • Lifetimes: @singleton, @transient, @scoped("request"), with exit stacks for cleanup
  • Factories: call_factory(), plus invoke() / ainvoke() for factories that mix injected and manual arguments
  • Async APIs: aget(), acall_factory(), ainvoke(), async_scope()
  • Modules and providers: Module, SimpleModule, ProviderModule, @provider
  • A resolver compiled per service (generated code, or plain closures with debug=True)
  • Safe under threads and asyncio tasks: the current container and scopes live in ContextVars, and reads take no lock
  • Integrations: InjectFastAPI, InjectFastMCP, InjectTaskiq (optional extras)
  • Diagnostics: dependency graph, validation, visualizer
  • Testing: container.override(...), override_dependency, isolated_container, InjectQ.test_mode()

docs.title: Factory with injected and manual arguments
docs.text:
def create_service(db: Database, cache: Cache, user_id: str):
    return UserService(db, cache, user_id)

container.bind_factory("user_service", create_service)

# db and cache are injected, user_id is passed by hand
service = container.invoke("user_service", user_id="user123")
service = await container.ainvoke("async_service", batch_size=100)  # async factories

See Factory Methods.

docs.title: Scopes and lifetimes
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ, singleton, transient, scoped

container = InjectQ.get_instance()

@singleton
class Database: ...        # one instance app-wide

@transient
class Validator: ...       # new instance every resolution

@scoped("request")
class RequestContext: ...  # one instance per request scope

with container.scope("request"):    # async: `async with container.async_scope("request"):`
    ctx1 = container.get(RequestContext)
    ctx2 = container.get(RequestContext)
    assert ctx1 is ctx2
# Outside the block, container.get(RequestContext) raises ScopeError

docs.title: FastAPI
docs.text:
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI
from injectq import InjectQ, singleton
from injectq.integrations.fastapi import setup_fastapi, InjectFastAPI

app = FastAPI()
container = InjectQ.get_instance()
setup_fastapi(container, app)

@singleton
class UserService:
    def get_user(self, user_id: int) -> dict:
        return {"id": user_id}

@app.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user(
    user_id: int,
    user_service: Annotated[UserService, InjectFastAPI(UserService)],
):
    return user_service.get_user(user_id)

docs.title: Taskiq
docs.text:
from typing import Annotated
from injectq import InjectQ
from injectq.integrations.taskiq import setup_taskiq, InjectTaskiq

container = InjectQ.get_instance()
setup_taskiq(container, broker)

@broker.task()

    service: Annotated[RankingService, InjectTaskiq(RankingService)],

docs.title: Modules and providers
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ
from injectq.modules import Module, SimpleModule, ProviderModule, provider

class AppModule(Module):
    def configure(self, binder):
        binder.bind(Config, Config())
        binder.bind(Database, Database)

class Services(SimpleModule):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.bind(UserService, UserService)

class Providers(ProviderModule):
    @provider
    def make_notifier(self, db: Database, cfg: Config) -> Notifier:
        return Notifier(db, cfg)

container = InjectQ(modules=[AppModule(), Services(), Providers()])

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
injectq compared with 13 other Python dependency injection libraries on the same object graphs. Every library first passes the same correctness checks, then is timed in its own process. Lower is better.

µs/op (median, lower is better) S1 singleton S2 transient chain S3 wide graph S4 request scope S5 injected call S6 async chain injectq 0.083 0.302 0.550 0.968 0.143 0.427 aioinject [1] 0.295 0.787 1.768 2.278 n/a 0.992 dependency-injector [2] 0.057 1.203 3.038 n/a 1.127 37.8 dishka [3] 0.307 0.516 1.069 1.526 1.165 1.068 diwire [4] 0.424 0.609 0.884 4.609 6.820 0.874 inject [5] 0.158 4.785 12.2 n/a 2.462 n/a injector [6] 1.331 42.7 90.6 14.4 16.8 n/a kink [7] 0.168 3.688 12.6 n/a 2.366 n/a lagom [8] 0.155 5.624 12.0 n/a 1.474 n/a punq [9] 1.097 36.5 90.6 n/a n/a n/a rodi [10] 0.290 0.758 1.852 0.836 1.056 n/a svcs [11] 0.189 2.590 8.087 1.940 n/a 3.068 that-depends [12] 0.077 0.938 3.479 24.7 3.163 1.569 wireup [13] 0.092 0.512 1.434 1.130 0.269 0.676 hand-written (floor) 0.019 0.166 0.355 0.345 0.041 0.229 injectq rank 3 of 14 1 of 14 1 of 14 2 of 9 1 of 11 1 of 8 fastest DI library dependency-injector injectq injectq rodi injectq injectq

Bold: fastest DI library in the column (hand-written excluded). n/a: the library has no such feature.

Setup notes per library ([1]-[13]) [1] **aioinject**: sync `SyncContainer` for S1-S5/S7, async `Container` for S6; transients registered in the lifetime scope to resolve from the root context. n/a: S5 no generic injection decorator (per-framework `inject` only). [2] **dependency-injector**: S6 uses providers in async mode. n/a: S4 no enter/exit request scope (only context-local singletons, a different mechanism). [3] **dishka**: no transient lifetime; `cache=False` is its equivalent. [4] **diwire**: default `SCOPED` lifetime at the root scope = singleton; transient via `Lifetime.TRANSIENT`; S5 passes `diwire_resolver=` explicitly. [5] **inject**: one global injector; singletons via `bind_to_constructor`, transients via `bind_to_provider`, constructors wired with `autoparams`. n/a: S4 no request scope; S6 no async resolution. [6] **injector**: request scope is a custom `Scope` subclass (cache swapped on enter/exit); constructors need `@inject` (applied to the benchmark classes). n/a: S6 no async API. [7] **kink**: `@inject` on a class registers it (singleton; `use_factory=True` = transient) and mutates `__init__`; S7 restores `__init__` before re-decorating. n/a: S4 no request scope; S6 no async resolution. [8] **lagom**: unregistered classes are autowired as transient. n/a: S4 no request scope; S6 no async resolution. [9] **punq**: transient is the default scope. n/a: S4 no request scope (only transient and singleton); S5 no injection decorator; S6 no async API. [10] **rodi**: resolved with `provider.get` / `provider.exec` (each call creates an activation scope); S7 includes `build_provider()`, which validates and wires eagerly. n/a: S6 no async resolution (sync only). [11] **svcs**: caches per `Container`, so transient = a new `Container` per operation (its construction is timed). n/a: S5 no generic injection decorator (framework integrations only). [12] **that-depends**: S5 with `@inject(scope=None)`; S4 via a `ContextResource` in `ContextScopes.REQUEST`. [13] **wireup**: transients and scoped services resolve from a scope: S2, S3, S6 use one long-lived scope, S4/S5 enter one per operation.

14 libraries, AMD Ryzen 5 5600G with Radeon Graphics, CPython 3.13.13, median of 25 repeats, 2026-11-23. Full table, chart and method: docs/benchmarks.md.

Scenarios: S1 resolve a cached singleton, S2 a 3-level transient chain, S3 a wide graph (5 transients sharing a singleton), S4 enter a request scope, resolve, exit, S5 call an @inject function with 3 dependencies, S6 S2 through the async API. Full tables, chart and method: Benchmarks. Raw JSON: benchmarks/results/.

Note

The tables, chart and machine details are generated by benchmarks/compare/report.py between the <!-- BENCH:... --> markers. Do not edit between the markers; re-run the benchmarks instead (see Reproduce).

docs.title: What is measured, and why
docs.text:
A container costs time in a few places. Each scenario isolates one of them.

Cost Scenario 1 Fetching something already built S1 2 Building an object graph on demand S2, S3, S6 3 Opening and closing a request scope S4 4 Injecting dependencies into a function call S5 5 Setting the container up S7

All numbers are microseconds per operation (lower is better). Every library resolves the same objects, and is compared with a hand-written baseline: plain constructor calls with no container. The baseline is the floor; the multiplier in the full table is the cost on top of it.

A container does not make your application faster. A web request usually spends tens or hundreds of microseconds in the framework, so 1 µs per request is rarely what you feel. See the HTTP benchmark for the end-to-end view.

docs.title: The scenarios
docs.text: The classes are tiny: constructors only store their arguments, so the measurement is the container.

docs.title: S1: cached singleton
docs.text:
Config is registered as a singleton. Measure container.get(Config) after it was created. Hand-written:

config = Config()
config            # "resolving" it

docs.title: S2: transient chain
docs.text:
C needs B, B needs A; all three are transient, so every resolve builds a fresh C, B and A. Hand-written:

C(B(A()))

docs.title: S3: wide graph
docs.text:
Wide takes five transient services D1..D5, and each Di takes its own singleton Si. Every resolve builds Wide and five Ds and reuses the five singletons. Hand-written:

Wide(D1(s1), D2(s2), D3(s3), D4(s4), D5(s5))

docs.title: S4: request scope
docs.text:
Enter a request scope, resolve Req (which needs the singleton Config), leave the scope. Inside one scope Req is the same object on repeat; a new scope gets a new one. Hand-written (a per-request cache, the smallest thing that meets this contract):

class RequestScope:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.cache = {}
        return self.req
    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        self.cache = None
    def req(self):
        r = self.cache.get(Req)
        if r is None:
            r = self.cache[Req] = Req(config)
        return r

with RequestScope() as req:
    req()

docs.title: S5: injected function call
docs.text:
f(x1: X1, x2: X2, x3: X3) where all three are singletons. Measure calling f() with no arguments and letting the library inject them. Hand-written:

f(x1, x2, x3)

docs.title: S6: async transient chain
docs.text:
The S2 graph, resolved from an async context (await container.aget(C) or the library's equivalent). Hand-written:

async def make_c():
    return C(B(A()))

docs.title: S7: build a container
docs.text:
Register 50 services in a chain (K0, K1(K0), ..., K49(K48)) in a fresh container. S7r additionally resolves K49 once, because some libraries do their graph analysis or code generation lazily on the first resolve, and building without resolving would hide that cost. Hand-written:

registry = {k: k for k in K}
obj = registry[K[0]]()
for k in K[1:]:
    obj = registry[k](obj)

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Same graph, verified. Every library script resolves its graph through a shared set of checks before timing anything (benchmarks/common.py, class Verifier): types and nesting are right, singletons are the same object across resolves, transients are fresh, request scope gives one instance per scope and different instances across scopes, the injected function receives the right singletons. A failed check aborts the run with a non-zero exit code. A library that cannot do something (for example no request scope) is reported as n/a, not approximated.
  • Process isolation. Each library runs in its own Python process, so imports, monkey-patching and caches of one library cannot affect another. Classes are created fresh per library.
  • Warm-up and calibration. One untimed call, then the loop count is calibrated so each repeat takes about 20 ms.
  • Repeats and statistic. The loop is timed BENCH_REPEATS times (25 by default); the median per-operation time is reported. Medians resist the occasional slow repeat caused by other processes.
  • Pinned versions. Library versions are pinned in benchmarks/compare/requirements.txt and recorded, with the CPU, OS and Python build, in the raw JSON under benchmarks/results/.
  • Equivalences that are not 1:1. Where a library has no direct equivalent, the closest idiomatic form is used and listed below.

docs.title: Equivalence notes
docs.text:
• hand-written is plain constructor calls with module-level singletons (S4 uses a minimal dict-backed per-request cache). It is the floor: no container, no resolution.
  • wireup: transients and request-scoped services can only be resolved from a scope. S2, S3 and S6 resolve from one long-lived scope; S4 enters and exits a scope per operation; S5 enters a scope per call (what inject_from_container does).
  • dishka has no transient lifetime: cache=False is its documented equivalent. All services except the request-scoped one are registered in Scope.APP.
  • svcs caches every service per Container, so "transient" is a fresh Container per operation (the container construction is part of the measured cost).
  • that-depends: S5 uses @inject(scope=None) (skips entering an inject scope on every call; the cheapest idiomatic form). S4 uses a ContextResource in ContextScopes.REQUEST.
  • injector: request scope is a custom Scope (the documented extension point), not a built-in. punq, kink and inject have no request scope (n/a). kink and inject wire classes by mutating __init__ / a global injector.
  • rodi: S7 includes build_provider() (eager validation and wiring), so S7 and S7r are the same cost. aioinject: SyncContainer for S1-S5/S7, async Container for S6. diwire: S5 passes diwire_resolver= explicitly because creating any other Container clears its global fallback.
  • lagom autowires unregistered classes as transients; the singletons and the 50-class chain are registered explicitly.
  • dependency-injector: S6 uses providers in async mode; Factory/Singleton providers are declared once, as in its docs.
  • S7 measures building the container; S7r additionally resolves the 50th service (a 50-deep chain), because some libraries defer work (graph analysis, code generation) to the first resolve.

docs.title: Where injectq is not the fastest
docs.text:
Generated from the same run, so it cannot drift from the tables:

  • S1 cached singleton: injectq is not fastest. dependency-injector takes 0.057 µs, injectq 0.083 µs (1.5x slower); injectq ranks 3 of 14.
  • S4 request scope: enter, resolve, exit: injectq is not fastest. rodi takes 0.836 µs, injectq 0.968 µs (1.2x slower); injectq ranks 2 of 9.
  • S7 build container (50 services): injectq is not fastest. inject takes 13.9 µs, injectq 27.4 µs (2.0x slower); injectq ranks 2 of 14.
  • S7r build container + resolve 50-deep chain: injectq is not fastest. inject takes 98.3 µs, injectq 251 µs (2.6x slower); injectq ranks 3 of 14.

Context to read these rows with:

  • S1 is a dictionary-style lookup of an already built object. dependency-injector is compiled (Cython), so on a pure lookup it can beat any pure-Python container. The absolute difference is small; see the table.
  • Libraries that make a scope the unit of work (for example wireup and dishka) can be faster than injectq at entering and leaving that scope or at injecting into a function; the table says by how much.

docs.title: HTTP benchmark
docs.text:
The micro-benchmarks measure the container alone. benchmarks/http/ measures it inside a real request: the same small FastAPI app for each library, served by one Uvicorn worker, hit by a load generator.

  • singleton endpoint: injects two long-lived services (A, B).
  • scoped endpoint: a request-scoped graph of seven services (C to I), some requested several times in one handler, with a generator resource (sync) and an async-generator resource that are torn down at the end of the request.
  • Before measuring, each app is started in a counting mode and checked: singletons built once, request-scoped services built once per request and torn down, 50 concurrent requests do not share request state. A library that fails is not measured.
  • Plain FastAPI Depends and a hand-wired app without DI are included as reference points.

(HTTP results not generated yet: run python benchmarks/http/run_http.py.)

Requests per second are for one worker on one machine; compare the ratios between rows, not the absolute values.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Micro-benchmarks. They measure the container, not your application. I/O and your own code usually dominate.
  • Author-written. The injectq authors wrote the script for each library from its documentation, using it idiomatically; deviations are listed above. A maintainer may know a faster way, and pull requests are welcome.
  • One CPython build, one machine. Other interpreters, free-threaded builds and CPUs can reorder the results. Ratios travel better than microseconds.
  • Features differ. Libraries trade off validation, async support, teardown and scopes. Faster is not the same as better for your needs.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/10xhub/injectq && cd injectq

# 1. micro-benchmarks, injectq only (uses your current environment)
python benchmarks/run.py                      # prints a table, writes benchmarks/latest.json
python benchmarks/check.py                    # fails if S1-S6 are >20% slower than the baseline

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to InjectQ are documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • validate() and compile() failed for factories that take call-time arguments (used with call_factory/get_factory). A factory whose parameters the container cannot fill is now skipped; resolving it with get()/aget()/@inject still raises. Cycles and classes depending on such a factory are still reported.

docs.title: [0.6.0] - Released
docs.text:
Focus: a new resolution engine, correct context and scope handling, and cleanup of the public API.

Upgrading from 0.5? Read the 0.6 migration guide. Benchmark numbers: see Benchmarks.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
Two bugs with the current container:

  • The current container leaked across asyncio tasks. It was stored in a place shared by every task on a thread, so one task could change the container another task saw. It is now a ContextVar: each task and thread has its own value.
  • The FastAPI request container was invisible to InjectQ.get_instance(). Code in a route that called get_instance() or used @inject got the global container. The middleware now makes the container current for the whole request. FastMCP and Taskiq work the same way.

Resolution and scopes:

  • aget() ignored the binding scope. Singletons were created again on every call and differed from get(). aget now honours scopes.
  • Concurrent aget calls raised a false CircularDependencyError, and a singleton could be created several times under concurrency. Both are fixed: cycles are found when the plan is built, and a singleton is created once.
  • aget(UnboundClass) returned an un-awaited coroutine.
  • A request scope never cleared. Two with container.scope("request") blocks returned the same instance, and request-scoped keys also resolved outside any scope.
  • Leaving a nested scope of the same name wiped the outer scope.
  • asyncio.to_thread inside a request got a different instance, which then leaked into the next request.
  • Scope exit dropped instances without closing them.
  • override() had no effect on factory-bound keys, cleared every singleton, was visible to all threads, and raised with allow_override=False.
  • A factory silently shadowed a later bind of the same key.
  • Integrations resolved with get(), so async factories were never awaited.
  • Resource teardown errors were swallowed, and two resources with the same function name replaced each other.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Typed resolution. container.get, aget, try_get and atry_get have @overloads: type[T] gives T, a str key gives Any, and try_* give T | None (or T | D with a default). Caveat: abstract classes as keys trigger mypy's type-abstract check.
  • New engine. Each service gets one compiled resolver, generated as Python code (or linked closures). Cycles, validation, compile() and the dependency graph all use the same plans. InjectQ(debug=True) switches to plain closures for simple tracebacks. Generated code is visible in tracebacks as <injectq-generated:Name>. See Debugging generated code.
  • Scopes. One request scope per with container.scope(...) or async with container.async_scope(...) block. ScopeError when a scoped key is resolved outside a scope. register_scope(name), current_exit_stack(scope). See Scoped services and Resources and cleanup.
  • Context. ContainerContext.set_current() and InjectQ.activate() return a token. ContainerContext.reset_current(token) restores the previous container. See Context and concurrency.
  • Overrides. container.override(key, value) is context-local, reaches dependents, works on factory keys and with allow_override=False, and only affects the overridden key. See Overrides.
  • @inject. Plans are built on first call (forward references work). Generators, async generators, classmethod and staticmethod in either order, partials and callable objects. Your own exceptions pass through unchanged. Error messages name the parameter.
  • Integrations. FastAPI, FastMCP and Taskiq enter a "request" scope per request, message or task and make the container current. New names: InjectFastMCP, setup_fastmcp, get_container_fastmcp, get_container_taskiq, InjectQTaskiqMiddleware. get_container_fastapi is exported and takes an optional connection. injectq.integrations is lazy.
  • Decorators and resources. @singleton, @transient, @scoped, @register_as and @resource work bare and with arguments. @resource binds the resource by its return annotation, with a scope. bind_factory(..., scope=...) and @provider(scope=...). container.shutdown(), await container.ashutdown() and container.track_resource(). Teardown errors are raised (ExceptionGroup on Python 3.11+).
  • Modules. ProviderModule scans the class dictionary, keeps definition order, awaits async providers in aget, and no longer hides errors.
  • Diagnostics. The validator and visualizer use the compiled plans. validate() reports cycles. The profiler is connected to the resolver (zero cost when none is attached), uses a bounded buffer and keeps its data across start() and stop(). attach_profiler() and detach_profiler(). injectq.utils.graph with find_cycles, find_path, reachable.
  • Testing. isolated_container, container_fixture(name=...), MockModule. test_mode() also sets the context container.
  • Exports. AlreadyRegisteredError, ModuleBinder, ResourceError and ScopeError from injectq. Diagnostics and testing load lazily.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
See the migration guide for before and after code.

  • The current container is per task and per thread. set_current() and activate() apply to the current task or thread and to what it starts, not to sibling tasks. Plain threads and run_in_executor do not inherit it.
  • Inside FastAPI, FastMCP and Taskiq handlers, get_instance() and @inject use the container given to setup_*.
  • get() on a key that needs an async factory raises InjectionError ("use aget") instead of returning a coroutine.
  • A request-scoped key resolved outside a scope raises ScopeError.
  • @inject no longer wraps your function's exceptions in InjectionError.
  • Inject[...] is a plain marker: no caching, side-effect-free repr.
  • One provider map: when a class and a factory are bound to the same key, the later registration wins. Re-binding a key drops its cached singleton.
  • A required constructor parameter with no annotation, or an unresolvable forward reference, raises InjectionError at the first resolve.
  • Parameter defaults are used only when the parameter's own key is not bound.
  • compile() raises on errors.
  • clear_scope() drops instances but does not run the exit stack.
  • Resources are created once under concurrency, and shut down in reverse order of creation.
  • InjectQMCPMiddleware no longer subclasses the FastMCP Middleware class.
  • Errors in integrations are raised, not logged first.

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text:
Removed in 0.7. They work now and emit DeprecationWarning.

  • injectq.testing: test_container (use isolated_container), TestModule (use MockModule), pytest_container_fixture (use container_fixture).
  • Integrations: InjectAPI (use InjectFastAPI), InjectTask (InjectTaskiq), InjectMCP (InjectFastMCP), setup_mcp (setup_fastmcp), get_container_mcp (get_container_fastmcp), get_injector_instance_taskiq (get_container_taskiq).
  • injectq.components and the Component* names exported from injectq.
  • InjectQ(thread_safe=...) and InjectQ(use_async_scopes=...): deprecated; accepted and ignored, and emit a DeprecationWarning when passed (removed in 0.7).

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• injectq.core.thread_safety (HybridLock, ThreadSafeDict, AsyncSafeCounter, ThreadSafetyMixin, thread_safe) and injectq.core.thread_safe_resolver.
  • injectq.core.async_scopes (AsyncScope, AsyncScopeManager, HybridScope, AsyncRequestScope, AsyncActionScope, request and user id helpers) and injectq.core.base_scope_manager. The scope names "async_request" and "async_action".
  • SingletonScope, TransientScope, ThreadLocalScope, RequestScope, ActionScope, create_enhanced_scope_manager and ScopeManager.get_scope().
  • The old DependencyResolver methods (resolve, resolve_async, validate_dependencies, get_dependency_graph, compile_resolution_plans).
  • Unused helpers in injectq.utils (resolve_forward_ref, Injected, is_concrete_type, get_type_name, safe_issubclass, is_injectable_function, ThreadLocalStorage) and the protocols Resolvable, InjectableFunction, InjectableAsyncFunction, AsyncInjectableCallable.
  • MissingDependencyError, InvalidBindingError, TypeMismatchError from injectq.diagnostics.validation.
  • injectq.integrations.fastapi._request_container.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• While an override() is active, that container resolves through slower guarded closures.
  • An override does not change objects that already hold the old singleton.
  • Free-threaded CPython is not tested.
  • On Python 3.15 the fastmcp extra cannot be installed yet (a dependency, rpds-py, does not build there).

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Benchmarks: compared with 13 other Python DI libraries, injectq 0.6 is fastest on transient chains, wide graphs, @inject calls and async resolution, 2nd on request scopes and 3rd on cached singletons. See Benchmarks.

docs.title: Reporting issues
docs.text:
Open an issue at github.com/10xhub/injectq/issues with:

  1. A description of the problem.
  2. The smallest code that reproduces it.
  3. What you expected and what happened (include the traceback).
  4. Python version, InjectQ version, OS, and the framework versions if an integration is involved.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
You need Python 3.10 or newer, uv and Git.

git clone https://github.com/<your-account>/injectq.git
cd injectq
uv sync                  # installs the project and the dev dependency group
pre-commit install       # optional: ruff, ruff-format, bandit and other hooks

Without uv: pip install -e ".[dev]". The dev extra covers tests, mypy and the integration frameworks (FastAPI, Taskiq, FastMCP). The documentation tools (MkDocs and plugins) are in the uv dev dependency group only.

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
uv run pytest                          # all tests
uv run pytest tests/v060/test_scopes.py   # one file
uv run pytest -k override              # by name
uv run ruff check .                    # lint (add --fix to fix)
uv run ruff format .                   # format
uv run mypy injectq                    # type check

pytest is configured in pyproject.toml: it always measures coverage of injectq and fails below 73%, and asyncio_mode = "auto" means async def tests need no marker.

make test runs uv run pytest -v. Other Makefile targets: make bench, make bench-compare and make bench-publish (see Benchmarks), make docs-serve and make docs-build.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Branch from main: git checkout -b feature/short-name (or fix/short-name).
  2. Make the change. Add or update tests, and update the docs if behaviour changed.
  3. Run uv run pytest, uv run ruff check . and uv run mypy injectq.
  4. Add an entry to the changelog for user-visible changes. A breaking change also needs a note in the migration guide (or the guide for the release it ships in).
  5. Push and open a pull request against main. Describe what changed and why, link related issues, and say how you tested it.

CI must pass and a maintainer must approve before a pull request is merged.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
• Ruff does linting and formatting (line length 88, isort-style imports). Type hints are required on public APIs and checked with mypy in strict mode.
  • Docstrings use the Google style.
  • Commit messages follow Conventional Commits: feat:, fix:, docs:, refactor:, test:, chore:, with an optional scope, for example fix(container): drop cached singleton on rebind.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Tests live in tests/. The 0.6 suite is in tests/v060/ (scopes, overrides, context, decorators, integrations, codegen, testing helpers). Older files sit directly in tests/. Put new tests next to the code they cover.

  • Use plain functions or classes named Test* with test_* methods.
  • Create a fresh InjectQ() in each test, or use isolated_container() / container_fixture() from injectq.testing, so tests share no bindings.
  • Do not import names that start with test_ or Test into a test module: pytest would try to collect them.
  • Run the suite with -W error::DeprecationWarning to catch use of deprecated names.
from injectq import InjectQ, inject


def test_inject_resolves_by_type():
    container = InjectQ()
    container.bind_instance("greeting", "hello")

    @inject(container=container)
    def handler(greeting: str) -> str:
        return f"{greeting}!"

    assert handler() == "hello!"


async def test_aget_creates_singleton_once():
    container = InjectQ()

    class Client: ...

    async def make() -> Client:
        return Client()

    container.bind_factory(Client, make, scope="singleton")
    assert await container.aget(Client) is await container.aget(Client)
