docs.title: The Container
docs.text:
An InjectQ container holds bindings (what to build for each key), builds objects from them, and caches them according to their scope.

from injectq import InjectQ

container = InjectQ()
container.bind(Database, PostgreSQLDatabase)    # key -> implementation
db = container.get(Database)                    # or container[Database]

Resolution looks up the binding, resolves each constructor parameter by its type hint, and builds the object. A concrete class that has no binding is built as-is, so you only need bind for abstractions, instances, factories and non-default scopes.

Inside InjectQ:

  • ServiceRegistry stores the bindings.
  • DependencyResolver compiles one resolver function per key. See Debugging generated code.
  • ScopeManager holds the singleton cache and the active scopes. See Service lifetimes.

docs.title: Which container is used
docs.text:
InjectQ.get_instance() returns the current container, or a global one if none is current. The @singleton, @transient, @scoped and @resource decorators, @inject and container.context() all work with it. You can use that global container, or create your own and make it current. Details: Context and concurrency.

from injectq import InjectQ, inject, singleton

@singleton                       # registers on InjectQ.get_instance()
class Database: ...

@singleton
class UserService:
    @inject
    def __init__(self, db: Database):
        self.db = db

@inject
def handler(service: UserService): ...

handler()

Tests should use a fresh container each time. See Testing.

docs.title: Dict-like
docs.text:
container["db_url"] = "postgresql://localhost/db"     # an instance under a string key
container[Database] = PostgreSQLDatabase               # a class

docs.title: bind
docs.text:
container.bind(Database, PostgreSQLDatabase)                    # singleton (default)
container.bind(Handler, Handler, scope="transient")
container.bind(RequestContext, RequestContext, scope="request")
container.bind_instance(Config, Config(debug=True))

A later binding of the same key replaces the earlier one (unless InjectQ(allow_override=False)).

docs.title: Factories
docs.text:
bind_factory runs a function to build the value. The function's own parameters are injected, and it is transient by default. Pass scope= to cache the result.

def create_database(config: DatabaseConfig) -> Database:
    return Database(config)

container.bind_factory(Database, create_database)                    # new value every get()
container.bind_factory(Database, create_database, scope="singleton")
db = container[Database]

An async def factory can only be resolved with await container.aget(...).

A factory can also take arguments you pass yourself. Call it with call_factory (all arguments yours) or invoke (injected parameters filled in, you supply the rest):

def create_pool(db_name: str, max_conn: int = 10) -> Pool: ...
container.bind_factory("db_pool", create_pool)

container.call_factory("db_pool", "users", max_conn=20)    # you pass every argument

def create_service(db: Database, user_id: str) -> UserService: ...
container.bind_factory("user_service", create_service)
container.invoke("user_service", user_id="u1")             # Database is injected
await container.ainvoke("user_service", user_id="u1")      # same, for async factories

get_factory(key) returns the function itself. A factory that needs caller arguments cannot be resolved with get(). validate() and compile() skip it. See Factory methods.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
A module groups bindings:

from injectq import InjectQ, Module

class DatabaseModule(Module):
    def configure(self, binder):
        binder.bind(Database, PostgreSQLDatabase)

container = InjectQ(modules=[DatabaseModule()])

See Modules.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
container.scope(name) and container.async_scope(name) open a scope. Keys bound to that scope are created once per block. Resolving them outside a block raises ScopeError.

with container.scope("request"):
    service = container.get(RequestService)

async with container.async_scope("request"):
    service = await container.aget(RequestService)

See Service lifetimes for the lifetimes and Scopes for the details.

docs.title: Checking and compiling
docs.text:
container.validate()    # InjectionError listing every key that cannot be built, including cycles (factories with call-time arguments are skipped)
container.compile()     # builds every resolver now; raises on any error (factories with call-time arguments are skipped)

Both run without creating your objects. Call one at startup to fail early. Resolving a cycle directly with get() raises CircularDependencyError.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
container.shutdown()             # or: await container.ashutdown()
container.clear()                # drop all bindings and cached instances

shutdown() closes singleton @resources in reverse order. Request-scoped resources close when their scope() block exits. container.context() only makes the container current and cleans nothing up. See Resources and cleanup.

docs.title: Replacing services in tests
docs.text:
with container.override(Database, FakeDatabase()):
    service = container.get(UserService)       # dependents see the fake too

injectq.testing adds isolated_container() and override_dependency(). See Overrides.

docs.title: Context and Concurrency
docs.text: This page explains which container InjectQ.get_instance(), @inject and the decorators use, and what that means for asyncio tasks and threads.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
InjectQ keeps the current container in a ContextVar. InjectQ.get_instance() returns the current container, or the global one if none is current.

A ContextVar has one value per execution context:

  • Each asyncio task runs in its own copy of the context it was created from.
  • A change made inside a task is not seen by other tasks.
  • A change made before a task starts is seen by that task.

So two tasks can work with two different containers at the same time, and neither one can leak into the other.

docs.title: Making a container current
docs.text:
Use a with block when you can. It always restores the previous value.

from injectq import InjectQ

container = InjectQ()

with container.context():
    assert InjectQ.get_instance() is container
# the previous container is back here

For async code, ContainerContext.use_async does the same job:

from injectq import ContainerContext

async def main():
    async with ContainerContext.use_async(container):
        await run_app()

When you cannot use a with block, activate() returns a token. Pass it to reset_current to restore the previous value:

from injectq import ContainerContext

token = container.activate()
try:
    ...
finally:
    ContainerContext.reset_current(token)

ContainerContext.set_current(container) does the same as activate(). ContainerContext.clear_current() sets the current container to None and cannot restore an outer value, so prefer tokens.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
A task sees the container that was current when the task was created.

import asyncio
from injectq import InjectQ

app = InjectQ()
other = InjectQ()


async def worker(name: str, container: InjectQ, ready: asyncio.Event, go: asyncio.Event):
    with container.context():
        ready.set()
        await go.wait()          # the other task runs now
        print(name, InjectQ.get_instance() is container)


async def main():
    e1, e2, go = asyncio.Event(), asyncio.Event(), asyncio.Event()
    t1 = asyncio.create_task(worker("A", app, e1, go))
    t2 = asyncio.create_task(worker("B", other, e2, go))
    await e1.wait()
    await e2.wait()
    go.set()
    await asyncio.gather(t1, t2)


asyncio.run(main())
# A True
# B True

A task you start after activating a container sees it:

token = app.activate()
try:
    result = await asyncio.create_task(child())   # child() sees `app`
finally:
    ContainerContext.reset_current(token)

A task that is already running does not see a later activate() made by another task.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
How the code runs Sees the caller's container? await asyncio.create_task(...) Yes await asyncio.to_thread(...) Yes anyio worker threads (anyio.to_thread.run_sync) Yes loop.run_in_executor(...) No: get_instance() returns the global container threading.Thread(...) No: get_instance() returns the global container

to_thread and anyio copy the caller's context to the worker thread. run_in_executor and threading.Thread do not.

If you must use run_in_executor or a plain thread, do one of these:

import contextvars

# 1. Copy the context yourself
ctx = contextvars.copy_context()
await loop.run_in_executor(None, ctx.run, work)

# 2. Or activate inside the thread
def work():
    with container.context():
        ...

Scopes follow the same rule. A with container.scope("request") block is visible to to_thread and to tasks started inside it. It is not visible to run_in_executor or plain threads. See Scoped services.

docs.title: Frameworks do this for you
docs.text:
setup_fastapi, setup_fastmcp and setup_taskiq make the container current for each request, message or task, and enter a "request" scope. Inside a handler, InjectQ.get_instance() and @inject use that container. See the FastAPI, FastMCP and Taskiq pages.

Sync Taskiq tasks are the one exception. Taskiq runs them with run_in_executor, so the container is not current in the task body. InjectTaskiq(...) parameters still work.

docs.title: Threads and singletons
docs.text:
Reading a bound singleton takes no lock. Creating a singleton takes a per-key lock, so the factory runs once even if many threads or tasks ask at the same time. Async factories share one future between all awaiters.

You do not need thread_safe=True. The argument is deprecated: it is accepted and ignored, and emits a DeprecationWarning.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
isolated_container() and InjectQ.test_mode() set the container as both the global instance and the current context container, then restore both:

from injectq.testing import isolated_container

def test_something():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container.bind(Database, FakeDatabase)
        ...

See Testing overview and Overrides.

docs.title: Debugging Generated Code
docs.text:
InjectQ 0.6 compiles each service into one Python function. For a Service that needs Repo, which needs Db, it builds a function that creates all three with plain constructor calls.

This page shows how to read that code and how to turn it off for simpler tracebacks.

docs.title: How a service gets compiled
docs.text:
1. The first get(Key) builds a plan for Key: its parameters, their types and scopes. Cycles are found here.
  2. Singleton keys use small linked closures. A singleton is created once, so generated code would not help.
  3. A transient or scoped key starts on closures. On its second resolve, it is replaced by one generated function. Dependencies that are transient are created inline, and singleton or scoped dependencies are read from the cache.
  4. container.compile() generates every resolver now. It also raises InjectionError if any registered service cannot be resolved, so it works as a startup check. A factory that needs arguments from the caller counts as unresolvable.

A change to the registry (a bind, an unbind, an override) throws the compiled code away. It is rebuilt on the next resolve.

docs.title: Reading the generated source
docs.text:
The resolver keeps the source of each generated function. Compile first, then ask for it:

from injectq import InjectQ


class Db: ...


class Repo:
    def __init__(self, db: Db) -> None:
        self.db = db


class Service:
    def __init__(self, repo: Repo, db: Db) -> None:
        self.repo = repo
        self.db = db


container = InjectQ()
container.bind(Db, Db, scope="singleton")
container.bind(Repo, Repo, scope="transient")
container.bind(Service, Service, scope="transient")

container.compile()
print(container._resolver.source(Service))

Output:

def resolve_Service():
    try:
        try:
            db = _singletons[key_Db]
        except _KeyError:
            db = _M
        if db is _M: db = resolve_Db()
        repo = Repo(db)
        try:
            db_2 = _singletons[key_Db]
        except _KeyError:
            db_2 = _M
        if db_2 is _M: db_2 = resolve_Db()
        return Service(repo, db_2)
    except _Exc as _e:
        _fail_at(_e, _lines, _root)

source() returns None when:

  • the key has not been compiled yet (call container.compile(), or resolve it twice),
  • the key is a singleton or an instance (they use closures),
  • you use InjectQ(debug=True),
  • a profiler is attached, or an override is active.

For an async resolver use source(key, is_async=True). It exists only for keys whose graph has an async factory.

Note

container._resolver is internal. Its layout can change in any release, and the printed code is for reading, not for parsing.

docs.title: Tracebacks
docs.text:
The generated code is registered with linecache under the file name <injectq-generated:Name>. Once a key has been compiled (after compile() or its second resolve), a failing constructor shows the generated line in the traceback:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<injectq-generated:Boom>", line 8, in resolve_Boom
    return Boom(db)
  File "app.py", line 4, in __init__
    raise RuntimeError("boom")
RuntimeError: boom

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
injectq.utils.exceptions.InjectionError: Failed to instantiate <class 'app.Boom'>: boom

Read it from the top:

  1. Your exception, and the generated line that called your constructor.
  2. InjectionError, raised once, for the class that failed. Its __cause__ is your exception. The same pattern applies to errors in factories.

InjectQ's own errors (CircularDependencyError, ScopeError, DependencyNotFoundError) are not wrapped.

docs.title: debug=True
docs.text:
container = InjectQ(debug=True)

With debug=True no code is generated. Resolution uses plain Python closures that call your constructors in order. You get:

  • Tracebacks whose frames are real source files (injectq/core/resolver.py and your code).
  • Code you can step through with a debugger.
  • source() returns None.

Closures are a little slower than generated code. Use debug=True while you debug and leave it off otherwise. See Benchmarks.

docs.title: Other helpers
docs.text:
container.validate()                   # raises InjectionError, lists every problem
container.get_dependency_graph()       # {key: [dependency keys]}
container.visualize_dependencies()     # DependencyVisualizer: to_dot(), to_ascii(), to_json()

injectq.utils.graph has find_cycles, find_path and reachable for graphs in this shape.

To time resolutions, use DependencyProfiler from injectq.diagnostics. It does not slow resolving when no profiler is attached.

docs.title: Service Lifetimes
docs.text:
A lifetime (scope) decides when an instance is created and how long it is shared.

Lifetime Instances Bind with Singleton (default) One per container @singleton, bind(K, Impl) Transient A new one on every resolve @transient, scope="transient" Scoped One per scope(...) block @scoped("request"), scope="request"

docs.title: Singleton
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ, singleton

@singleton
class Database: ...

container = InjectQ.get_instance()
assert container.get(Database) is container.get(Database)

Use it for shared, expensive or stateless services: connection pools, configuration, clients. A singleton is created once even when many threads or tasks ask at the same time. It must not hold per-request state, and any mutable state it holds must be safe to share.

docs.title: Transient
docs.text:
from injectq import transient

@transient
class Validator: ...

assert container.get(Validator) is not container.get(Validator)

Use it for cheap objects with their own state.

docs.title: Scoped
docs.text:
Built-in scope names are "request" and "action". Open a scope with with container.scope(name) (or async with container.async_scope(name)). Each block gets its own instances.

from injectq import InjectQ, scoped

@scoped("request")                  # bare @scoped means "request"
class RequestContext:
    user_id: int | None = None

container = InjectQ.get_instance()

with container.scope("request"):
    a = container.get(RequestContext)
    assert a is container.get(RequestContext)       # same inside the block

with container.scope("request"):
    assert container.get(RequestContext) is not a  # new block, new instance

container.get(RequestContext)                      # ScopeError: no active 'request' scope

Nested blocks with the same name restore the outer scope when they exit. setup_fastapi, setup_fastmcp and setup_taskiq open a "request" scope for each request, message or task.

A singleton cannot depend on a scoped service in a useful way: it would capture the instance from the first scope that created it.

docs.title: Custom scopes
docs.text:
A custom scope is a name you register:

container.register_scope("job")

@scoped("job")
class JobContext: ...

with container.scope("job"):
    job = container.get(JobContext)
    container.current_exit_stack("job").callback(print, "job finished")

Entering a name that was never registered raises ScopeError. The callback runs when the block exits. For resources with cleanup, use @resource("request"). See Resources and cleanup.

docs.title: Binding without decorators
docs.text:
from injectq import ScopeType

container.bind(RequestContext, RequestContext, scope=ScopeType.REQUEST)
container.bind(Validator, Validator, scope=ScopeType.TRANSIENT)
container.bind(JobContext, JobContext, scope="job")

docs.title: Choosing a lifetime
docs.text:
• Shared and safe to share: singleton.
  • Holds data for one request, job or operation: scoped.
  • Cheap, with its own state: transient.

Putting per-request data in a singleton is the usual mistake. Every request then sees the same object.

docs.title: Testing lifetimes
docs.text:
import pytest
from injectq import ScopeError
from injectq.testing import isolated_container

def test_scoped():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container.bind(RequestContext, RequestContext, scope="request")

        with pytest.raises(ScopeError):
            container.get(RequestContext)

        with container.scope("request"):
            assert container.get(RequestContext) is container.get(RequestContext)

Further reading: Singleton, Transient, Scoped services, Understanding scopes.

docs.title: Type Safety
docs.text: InjectQ resolves dependencies from type hints, and the package ships a py.typed marker, so mypy and pyright read its types.

docs.title: Resolution from type hints
docs.text:
A constructor parameter is resolved by its annotation. @inject does the same for function parameters.

from injectq import inject, singleton

@singleton
class Database:
    def query(self, sql: str) -> list[dict]:
        return []

@singleton
class UserService:
    @inject
    def __init__(self, db: Database) -> None:
        self.db = db

@inject
def process(service: UserService) -> None:
    ...

A parameter with no annotation and no default raises InjectionError. Give it a type hint or a default.

docs.title: Typed get
docs.text:
get, aget, try_get and atry_get have overloads, so a type checker knows what you get back:

Call Type container.get(UserService) UserService container.get("db_url") Any container.try_get(UserService) UserService \| None container.try_get(UserService, default) UserService \| type(default)

container[UserService] returns Any. Use get where you want checking.

The overloads take type[T], so mypy's type-abstract check flags an abstract class or Protocol used as a key. Silence it on that line with # type: ignore[type-abstract].

docs.title: Protocols and abstract classes as keys
docs.text:
Bind the abstraction to an implementation. A Protocol or ABC cannot be built, so without a binding resolution raises InjectionError.

from typing import Protocol

class DatabaseProtocol(Protocol):
    def query(self, sql: str) -> list[dict]: ...

class PostgreSQLDatabase:
    def query(self, sql: str) -> list[dict]:
        return []

class UserService:
    def __init__(self, db: DatabaseProtocol) -> None:
        self.db = db

container.bind(DatabaseProtocol, PostgreSQLDatabase)
service = container.get(UserService)

In a test, bind a fake to the same key:

from injectq.testing import isolated_container

def test_user_service():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container.bind(DatabaseProtocol, FakeDatabase)
        ...

docs.title: Errors found before runtime
docs.text:
validate() builds the plan for every registered key without creating objects. It reports missing bindings and cycles together in one InjectionError. compile() does the same and also generates the resolvers.

from injectq import InjectQ, InjectionError

class Client:
    def __init__(self, url: str) -> None: ...      # no binding for "str"

container = InjectQ()
container.bind(Client, Client)

try:
    container.validate()
except InjectionError as e:
    print(e)
    # Dependency validation failed:
    #   - Client: No binding found for type: <class 'str'>

Call one of them at startup. A cycle found by get() directly raises CircularDependencyError. Parameters with defaults are valid.

A forward reference such as "Cache" is resolved when the plan is built, so it must be importable from the class's module by then.

docs.title: What is Dependency Injection?
docs.text: Dependency injection (DI) means an object receives the things it depends on instead of creating them itself.

docs.title: Without and with DI
docs.text:
class UserService:
    def __init__(self):
        self.db = Database()      # hard-wired: cannot swap or fake it in a test
        self.cache = Cache()

class UserService:
    def __init__(self, db: Database, cache: Cache):
        self.db = db
        self.cache = cache

service = UserService(Database(), Cache())    # wired in one place

The second form is easy to test (pass fakes), and you can change an implementation without touching UserService. The place where objects are created and connected is called the composition root.

docs.title: What a container adds
docs.text:
Wiring by hand gets repetitive as the graph grows: UserService needs Database and Cache, Database needs a config, and so on. A DI container reads the type hints of each constructor and builds the whole graph for you.

from injectq import InjectQ, inject

container = InjectQ()
container.bind(Cache, RedisCache)      # map an abstraction to an implementation
# Database and UserService are concrete classes, so they need no binding

@inject
def process_user(service: UserService):
    ...

with container.context():              # make this container the current one
    process_user()                     # UserService, Database and Cache are built for you

The container controls object creation. Your code only declares what it needs. This is "inversion of control".

docs.title: Kinds of injection
docs.text:
• Constructor injection passes dependencies to __init__. Use it by default: dependencies are explicit, and a missing one fails when the object is built. InjectQ resolves constructor parameters from their type hints.
  • Function injection passes dependencies to a function with @inject. See @inject.
  • Property and method injection set dependencies after construction or per call. They hide what an object needs, so InjectQ does not do them for you.

docs.title: Things to avoid
docs.text:
• Service locator: calling container.get(Database) inside a class body. The dependency is hidden from the constructor signature and from tests. Ask for it in __init__ instead.
  • Circular dependencies: A needs B and B needs A. InjectQ raises CircularDependencyError. Break the cycle by extracting a third class or by passing the value at call time.

Next: the container.

docs.title: Your First App
docs.text: A small user-management app, built in layers (config, database, repository, service), wired together by InjectQ. It runs as a script and has tests.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
my_injectq_app/
├── __init__.py
├── models.py
├── config.py
├── database.py
├── repository.py
├── service.py
└── main.py
tests/
└── test_user_service.py

Run everything from the directory that contains my_injectq_app/.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
# my_injectq_app/models.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime


@dataclass
class User:
    id: int | None
    username: str
    email: str
    created_at: datetime
    is_active: bool = True

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
# my_injectq_app/config.py
from injectq import singleton


@singleton
class AppConfig:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.app_name = "User Management"
        self.max_users = 100

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
# my_injectq_app/database.py
from injectq import singleton

from .config import AppConfig
from .models import User


@singleton
class Database:
    """In-memory store standing in for a real database."""

    def __init__(self, config: AppConfig) -> None:
        self.config = config
        self._users: dict[int, User] = {}
        self._next_id = 1

    async def save(self, user: User) -> User:
        if len(self._users) >= self.config.max_users:
            raise ValueError("user limit reached")
        user.id = self._next_id
        self._next_id += 1
        self._users[user.id] = user
        return user

    async def find_by_username(self, username: str) -> User | None:
        return next((u for u in self._users.values() if u.username == username), None)

    async def all(self) -> list[User]:
        return list(self._users.values())

Database asks for an AppConfig in its constructor. InjectQ reads the type hint and passes the singleton.

docs.title: Repository and service
docs.text:
# my_injectq_app/repository.py
from datetime import datetime

from injectq import singleton

from .database import Database
from .models import User


@singleton
class UserRepository:
    def __init__(self, db: Database) -> None:
        self.db = db

    async def create(self, username: str, email: str) -> User:
        user = User(id=None, username=username, email=email, created_at=datetime.now())
        return await self.db.save(user)

    async def get_by_username(self, username: str) -> User | None:
        return await self.db.find_by_username(username)

    async def list_all(self) -> list[User]:
        return await self.db.all()

# my_injectq_app/service.py
from injectq import singleton

from .models import User
from .repository import UserRepository


class UserAlreadyExistsError(Exception):
    pass


@singleton
class UserService:
    def __init__(self, repo: UserRepository) -> None:
        self.repo = repo

    async def create_user(self, username: str, email: str) -> User:
        if await self.repo.get_by_username(username):
            raise UserAlreadyExistsError(username)
        return await self.repo.create(username, email)

    async def list_users(self) -> list[User]:
        return await self.repo.list_all()

No manual bindings are needed. @singleton registers each class when its module is imported, and UserService -> UserRepository -> Database -> AppConfig is resolved from the constructor type hints.

docs.title: Entry point
docs.text:
# my_injectq_app/main.py
import asyncio

from injectq import inject

from .config import AppConfig
from .service import UserAlreadyExistsError, UserService


@inject
async def run(service: UserService, config: AppConfig) -> None:
    print(config.app_name)
    await service.create_user("john_doe", "john@example.com")
    await service.create_user("jane_smith", "jane@example.com")
    try:
        await service.create_user("john_doe", "other@example.com")
    except UserAlreadyExistsError as exc:
        print(f"Rejected duplicate: {exc}")
    for user in await service.list_users():
        print(f"{user.id}: {user.username} <{user.email}>")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(run())

@inject works on async functions. Calling run() with no arguments resolves UserService and AppConfig from the global container.

python -m my_injectq_app.main

User Management
Rejected duplicate: john_doe
1: john_doe <john@example.com>
2: jane_smith <jane@example.com>

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Replace the repository with a fake inside isolated_container(). The container is fresh for the block and the previous one is restored afterwards. container[UserService] = UserService binds the class so it is built from the fake repository.

# tests/test_user_service.py
import pytest

from injectq.testing import isolated_container
from my_injectq_app.models import User
from my_injectq_app.repository import UserRepository
from my_injectq_app.service import UserAlreadyExistsError, UserService


class FakeRepository:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.users: dict[str, User] = {}

    async def get_by_username(self, username):
        return self.users.get(username)

    async def create(self, username, email):
        user = User(id=len(self.users) + 1, username=username, email=email, created_at=None)
        self.users[username] = user
        return user


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_create_user():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container[UserRepository] = FakeRepository()
        container[UserService] = UserService
        service = container[UserService]
        user = await service.create_user("test", "test@example.com")
        assert user.username == "test"


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_duplicate_username():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container[UserRepository] = FakeRepository()
        container[UserService] = UserService
        service = container[UserService]
        await service.create_user("test", "a@example.com")
        with pytest.raises(UserAlreadyExistsError):
            await service.create_user("test", "b@example.com")

Run with pytest (async tests need pytest-asyncio, included in injectq[dev]).

docs.title: Python versions
docs.text:
InjectQ needs Python 3.10 or newer and is tested on 3.10 through 3.15.

Python 3.15 explicit lazy imports (PEP 810) work with InjectQ 0.5.0 and later. If you enable them, a module imported only to run @singleton, @register_as or container.bind(...) is no longer loaded, so its services are not registered. See Python 3.15 Lazy Imports.

class A:
    pass

container[A] = A()

assert container.get(A) is container[A]

docs.title: Python 3.15 Lazy Imports
docs.text: Python 3.15 adds explicit lazy imports (PEP 810). A lazy import loads the module the first time your code uses a name from it, which can speed up startup. A runnable demo is in examples/python315_lazy_imports/.

docs.title: Do I need to change anything?
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 to 3.14, or 3.15 without lazy imports: no.
  • Python 3.15 with lazy imports: use InjectQ 0.5.0 or later, and check how your services get registered (see Registration side effects).

InjectQ 0.4.2 and earlier fail under global lazy mode with TypeError: 'module' object is not callable when @inject, @singleton or @resource is applied. 0.5.0 fixed this.

docs.title: Turning lazy imports on
docs.text:
Per module, with __lazy_modules__ (safe on every version; older Pythons ignore it):

__lazy_modules__ = ["reports"]

import reports  # lazy on 3.15, normal on 3.10-3.14
from injectq import InjectQ, inject

Per import, with the lazy keyword (3.15 only; a SyntaxError on older versions):

lazy import reports

Globally, for the whole process:

PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS=all python app.py
# or
python -X lazy_imports=all app.py

Global mode makes nearly every import in every package lazy. It has the biggest effect on startup and is the mode most likely to expose the problem below. Lazy imports help most for your own slow modules. import injectq is already fast.

docs.title: Registration side effects
docs.text:
These register a service when the module that defines it is imported:

  • @singleton, @transient, @scoped and @register_as(...) on a class
  • top-level container.bind(...) or container[Key] = value

A common pattern is to import such a module only for that effect:

# services.py
from injectq import register_as
from interfaces import Notifier

@register_as(Notifier)
class EmailNotifier(Notifier):
    def send(self, message: str) -> str:
        return f"email sent: {message}"

# app.py
import services  # imported only so @register_as runs
from injectq import InjectQ
from interfaces import Notifier

InjectQ.get_instance().get(Notifier)

Under lazy imports, import services doesn't load the module and nothing uses a name from it, so the decorator never runs:

injectq.utils.exceptions.DependencyNotFoundError: No binding found for type: <class 'interfaces.Notifier'>

This happens with global lazy mode, or when the module is in __lazy_modules__ or imported with lazy import. It does not happen when you resolve the concrete class (container.get(EmailNotifier)), because using the name loads the module.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
Make sure every registering module is loaded before you resolve. Each of these works on every Python version.

Load it with importlib. A function call always runs immediately:

import importlib

importlib.import_module("services")

Exclude it from lazy loading. In your entry point, before other imports, install a filter that returns False for modules that must stay eager:

import sys

REGISTRATION_MODULES = {"services"}

if hasattr(sys, "set_lazy_imports_filter"):  # Python 3.15+
    sys.set_lazy_imports_filter(
        lambda _importer, name, _fromlist: name not in REGISTRATION_MODULES
    )

import services  # now always loaded right away

With __lazy_modules__, just don't list the registering modules.

Register explicitly at startup. Put bindings in a function and call it. Calling the function loads its module, and the bound classes need no decorators:

# sms.py
from interfaces import Notifier

class SmsNotifier(Notifier):
    def send(self, message: str) -> str:
        return f"sms sent: {message}"

# wiring.py
from injectq import InjectQ
from interfaces import Notifier
from sms import SmsNotifier

def setup_container() -> None:
    InjectQ.get_instance().bind(Notifier, SmsNotifier)

# app.py
from wiring import setup_container

setup_container()

docs.title: Before using global mode in production
docs.text: Global mode changes imports for every library, and not all support it yet (pytest currently fails to start under PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS=all). Run the full application with it in a test environment and resolve each registered service at least once.

docs.title: Hello world
docs.text:
from injectq import inject, singleton

@singleton
class UserService:
    def greet(self) -> str:
        return "Hello from InjectQ!"

@inject
def main(service: UserService) -> None:
    print(service.greet())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

@singleton registers the class with the global container (InjectQ.get_instance()). @inject fills in parameters that have a registered type.

docs.title: Services with dependencies
docs.text:
Constructor parameters are resolved from their type hints. Decorate the class and the container builds the whole chain.

from injectq import inject, singleton

@singleton
class Database:
    def query(self, sql: str) -> str:
        return f"Result of: {sql}"

@singleton
class UserService:
    @inject
    def __init__(self, db: Database):
        self.db = db

    def get_users(self) -> str:
        return self.db.query("SELECT * FROM users")

@inject
def show_users(service: UserService) -> None:
    print(service.get_users())

show_users()  # Result of: SELECT * FROM users

docs.title: Three ways to get a service
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ, inject

# 1. Decorator (recommended)
@inject
def my_function(service: UserService) -> None: ...

container = InjectQ.get_instance()

# 2. Dict-like
container["config"] = "prod"
container[Database] = Database()
config = container["config"]

# 3. Explicit
service = container.get(UserService)

docs.title: Lifetimes
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ, inject, singleton, transient, scoped

@singleton   # one instance for the whole container
class Logger: ...

@transient   # a new instance on every resolution
class Handler:
    @inject
    def __init__(self, logger: Logger):
        self.logger = logger

@scoped("request")   # one instance per scope block
class RequestContext: ...

container = InjectQ.get_instance()

assert container[Logger] is container[Logger]
assert container[Handler] is not container[Handler]
assert container[Handler].logger is container[Handler].logger

# Scoped services only resolve inside a scope
with container.scope("request"):            # async: `async with container.async_scope("request"):`
    assert container.get(RequestContext) is container.get(RequestContext)

See Understanding Scopes.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
Group related bindings in a Module and pass the modules to the container.

from injectq import InjectQ, Module

class Database: ...
class UserService:
    def __init__(self, db: Database):
        self.db = db

class AppModule(Module):
    def configure(self, binder):
        binder.bind(Database, Database)
        binder.bind(UserService, UserService)

container = InjectQ(modules=[AppModule()])
service = container.get(UserService)

@inject uses the global container. A container you create yourself is used through container.get(...), or by making it current with with container.context():. See Modules.

docs.title: Factory with injected arguments
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ, inject

container = InjectQ.get_instance()
container["db_url"] = "postgresql://localhost/db"

class Database:
    def __init__(self, url: str):
        self.url = url

@inject
def create_database(db_url: str) -> Database:
    return Database(db_url)

container.bind_factory(Database, create_database)

db = container[Database]   # create_database runs with db_url injected

docs.title: Factory with manual arguments
docs.text:
call_factory() passes your arguments straight to the factory.

def create_cache(namespace: str, ttl: int = 3600):
    return RedisCache(namespace, ttl)

container.bind_factory("cache", create_cache)

users = container.call_factory("cache", "users", ttl=7200)
sessions = container.call_factory("cache", "sessions")

docs.title: Mixed: invoke()
docs.text:
invoke() injects the parameters you don't pass. Pass the manual ones as keyword arguments.

def create_user_service(db: Database, cache: Cache, user_id: str) -> UserService:
    return UserService(db, cache, user_id)

container.bind_factory("user_service", create_user_service)

service = container.invoke("user_service", user_id="user123")   # db and cache injected

# async factories
result = await container.ainvoke("async_service", batch_size=100)

See Factory Methods.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ, inject, singleton
from injectq.testing import isolated_container, override_dependency

@singleton
class Database:
    def get_user(self, user_id: int):
        return {"id": user_id, "name": "Real User"}

@singleton
class UserService:
    @inject
    def __init__(self, db: Database):
        self.db = db

    def get_user(self, user_id: int):
        return self.db.get_user(user_id)

class MockDatabase:
    def get_user(self, user_id: int):
        return {"id": user_id, "name": "Mock User"}

def test_with_isolated_container():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container[Database] = MockDatabase()
        container[UserService] = UserService
        assert container[UserService].get_user(1)["name"] == "Mock User"

def test_with_override():
    with override_dependency(Database, MockDatabase()):
        service = InjectQ.get_instance().get(UserService)
        assert service.get_user(1)["name"] == "Mock User"
  • isolated_container() gives each test a fresh container and restores the old one afterwards.
  • override_dependency() temporarily replaces one binding.

See Testing.

docs.title: Dict-like Interface
docs.text:
The container works like a dictionary. It is the shortest way to register and fetch services.

from injectq import InjectQ

container = InjectQ.get_instance()

container["database_url"] = "postgresql://localhost/db"   # a value
container["config"] = {"debug": False}                    # any object

url = container["database_url"]

docs.title: What assignment does
docs.text:
You assign Result A class: container[Database] = Database Bound as a singleton. Its constructor parameters are resolved from the container. Anything else Bound as an instance and returned as is. 
class DatabaseConfig:
    def __init__(self):
        self.host = "localhost"

class Database:
    def __init__(self, config: DatabaseConfig):
        self.config = config

container[DatabaseConfig] = DatabaseConfig
container[Database] = Database

db = container[Database]          # DatabaseConfig is built and injected
assert db is container[Database]  # singleton

For a different scope, use container.bind(Key, Impl, scope="transient"). See Scopes.

Assigned values are not called

container["now"] = lambda: datetime.now() stores the lambda itself. To compute a value on every lookup, use bind_factory.

Instances also register their own type

Assigning an instance under a string key also binds type(instance) to it, replacing any earlier binding of that type. After container["a"] = "x", container[str] returns "x". Prefer string keys for plain values such as str and int, and avoid container[str] = ....

docs.title: Other operations
docs.text:
"database_url" in container       # True if bound
del container["database_url"]     # remove a binding; KeyError if there is none
container.get("database_url")     # same as container[...]
container.try_get("missing")      # None instead of raising

Looking up a key that is not bound and cannot be built raises DependencyNotFoundError.

docs.text:
from injectq.testing import isolated_container

def test_user_service():

        container[Database] = FakeDatabase()
        container[UserService] = UserService

        assert container[UserService].get_user(1) is not None

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use it for configuration values, small apps and quick scripts. For many services, scopes or explicit contracts, move to bind, decorators and modules. The container is the same, so you can mix styles.

Next: the @inject decorator

docs.title: Factory Methods
docs.text:
A factory is a function that builds a service. Bind it with bind_factory. There are three ways to use one, depending on where its arguments come from.

Arguments come from Use The container get() / aget() The caller call_factory() / acall_factory() Both invoke() / ainvoke()

docs.title: Factories with injection
docs.text:
The factory's parameters are injected like a constructor's. get() calls the factory.

from injectq import InjectQ

container = InjectQ()
container.bind("db_url", "postgresql://localhost/mydb")
container.bind(Cache, Cache)

def create_user_service(db_url: str, cache: Cache) -> UserService:
    return UserService(db_url, cache)

container.bind_factory(UserService, create_user_service)

service = container[UserService]

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
By default the factory runs on every get() (transient). Pass scope to cache the result:

container.bind_factory(Database, create_database, scope="singleton")      # built once
container.bind_factory(Session, create_session, scope="request")          # once per request scope

docs.title: Async factories
docs.text:
An async def factory can only be resolved with aget(). Calling get() on it raises InjectionError.

async def create_database(db_url: str) -> Database:
    return await Database.connect(db_url)

container.bind_factory(Database, create_database, scope="singleton")

db = await container.aget(Database)

If the result is already cached (singleton, or scoped in the active scope), get() returns it.

docs.title: Registration order
docs.text: The last registration of a key wins, whether it came from bind, bind_instance or bind_factory. With InjectQ(allow_override=False) the second registration raises AlreadyRegisteredError.

docs.title: Factories with caller arguments
docs.text:
When the arguments come from the caller, do not use get(). It would try to inject them and fail. Fetch the raw function instead:

def create_pool(db_name: str, max_conn: int = 10) -> ConnectionPool:
    return ConnectionPool(db_name, max_conn)

container.bind_factory("db_pool", create_pool)

pool = container.call_factory("db_pool", "users_db", max_conn=20)

# or in two steps
factory = container.get_factory("db_pool")
pool = factory("users_db", max_conn=20)

call_factory calls the function directly. Nothing is cached, whatever scope the binding has. get_factory and call_factory raise DependencyNotFoundError if no factory is bound under the key.

Async versions:

pool = await container.acall_factory("async_pool", "users_db", max_conn=20)

factory = await container.aget_factory("async_pool")
pool = await factory("users_db")

acall_factory awaits the result if the factory is async def. aget_factory only looks the function up, so you must await its result yourself.

This pattern suits several instances with different settings:

container.bind_factory("cache", lambda namespace, ttl=3600: RedisCache(namespace, ttl))

users = container.call_factory("cache", "users", ttl=7200)
sessions = container.call_factory("cache", "sessions")

docs.title: Both: invoke()
docs.text:
invoke() calls the factory with the arguments you pass and injects the rest.

container.bind("api_key", "secret-123")
container.bind(RateLimiter, RateLimiter)

def create_api_client(
    api_key: str,
    rate_limiter: RateLimiter,
    timeout: int = 30,
    user_id: str = "",
) -> APIClient:
    return APIClient(api_key, rate_limiter, timeout, user_id)

container.bind_factory("client", create_api_client)

client = container.invoke("client", user_id="u1", timeout=60)

For each parameter that you did not pass:

  1. An Inject[...] default is resolved.
  2. If a key with the parameter's name is bound, it is injected.
  3. Otherwise, if the annotation is a bound type, it is injected. Primitive annotations (str, int, float, bool) are never matched by type, so several int bindings stay unambiguous. They are injected by name only.
  4. Otherwise the parameter's default is used.
  5. A required parameter that cannot be filled raises DependencyNotFoundError.

Pass your own arguments by keyword. Positional arguments are matched in order and skip injection for those parameters.

Async factories work the same way with await container.ainvoke(...).

docs.title: Example: pools that share settings
docs.text:
container.bind("db_host", "localhost")
container.bind("max_connections", 10)

def create_pool(db_name: str, db_host: str, max_connections: int) -> ConnectionPool:
    return ConnectionPool(db_name, db_host, max_connections)

container.bind_factory("db_pool", create_pool)

users = container.invoke("db_pool", db_name="users_db")
orders = container.invoke("db_pool", db_name="orders_db", max_connections=20)

If every parameter comes from the container, use get(). If none do, use call_factory().

docs.title: @inject Decorator
docs.text:
@inject fills in a function's parameters from the container, based on their type hints. Call the function without those arguments.

from injectq import InjectQ, inject

container = InjectQ.get_instance()
container[Database] = Database
container[UserService] = UserService

@inject
def process_user(service: UserService, db: Database) -> None:
    db.save(service.get_user(1))

process_user()    # service and db are injected

Dependencies of dependencies are built too. A class with no binding and an injectable constructor is built automatically.

docs.title: How parameters are resolved
docs.text:
For each parameter, in this order:

  1. An argument you pass wins. Only missing parameters are injected.
  2. An Inject[...] default marks the key explicitly (see below).
  3. A bound key with the same name as the parameter.
  4. The type annotation.
  5. The parameter's default value, for parameters that cannot be built (such as retries: int = 3).

A bound protocol works like any other key:

container.bind(IUserRepository, UserRepository)

@inject
def get_user(repo: IUserRepository):
    return repo.get_by_id(1)

docs.title: Inject[...]
docs.text:
Use it to inject a key that is not the annotation, such as a string key:

from injectq import Inject, inject

container["db_url"] = "postgresql://localhost/app"

@inject
def connect(url: str = Inject["db_url"]) -> None:
    ...

An Inject[...] marker beats a bound key that matches the parameter name. If the key cannot be resolved, the call raises. The marker is plain data: it does not cache anything, and repr() does not resolve it. Outside @inject, an Inject[T] value resolves from the current container each time you read an attribute on it.

docs.title: What it can decorate
docs.text:
• Sync and async functions (await process(...) works as usual).
  • Generators and async generators. Injection happens on the first next().
  • Methods. self and cls are skipped. @classmethod and @staticmethod work in either order with @inject.
  • __init__, so a class can receive injected constructor parameters when you call UserController().
  • functools.partial objects and callable objects.
class UserController:
    @inject
    def __init__(self, service: UserService, logger: Logger):
        self.service = service
        self.logger = logger

controller = UserController()

The injection plan is built on the first call, not at decoration time. Forward references and from __future__ import annotations therefore work, and the decorator can run before the services are bound.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Your own exceptions pass through unchanged. @inject does not wrap them:

@inject
def handler(repo: UserRepository) -> None:
    raise ValueError("bad input")

try:
    handler()
except ValueError:
    ...    # not InjectionError

A failure to resolve a parameter raises InjectionError. The message names the function and the parameter, and __cause__ holds the original error:

@inject
def connect(url: str) -> None: ...

connect()
# InjectionError: Cannot inject parameter 'url' of connect: No binding found for type: <class 'str'>
# connect() raised from DependencyNotFoundError

A dependency cycle raises CircularDependencyError unchanged.

docs.title: Which container
docs.text:
@inject uses the current container: InjectQ.get_instance(), or the one set with container.activate() or with container.context():. Inside FastAPI, FastMCP and Taskiq handlers it is the container you passed to setup_*. See Context and concurrency.

Request-scoped dependencies need an active scope. Frameworks enter one per request. In plain code, wrap the call in with container.scope("request"):.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
from injectq.testing import isolated_container

def test_get_user():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container[UserService] = FakeUserService()

        @inject
        def get_user(service: UserService):
            return service.get_user(1)

        assert get_user() is not None

To replace a service for the duration of a block, use container.override.

Next: Factory methods | Testing

docs.title: Parameterized Factories
docs.text:
InjectQ supports two types of factory functions:

  1. Dependency Injection (DI) Factories - Factories whose parameters are automatically resolved from the container
  2. Parameterized Factories - Factories that accept custom arguments passed by the caller

This flexibility allows you to choose the right pattern for your use case.

docs.title: 📋 Table of Contents
docs.text:
• DI Factories (Auto-Resolution)
  • Parameterized Factories (Manual Arguments)
  • API Methods
  • Use Cases
  • Best Practices

docs.title: DI Factories (Auto-Resolution)
docs.text: These are the traditional factory functions where InjectQ automatically resolves all parameters from the container.

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ
from datetime import datetime

container = InjectQ()

# Factory with no parameters
container.bind_factory("timestamp", lambda: datetime.now().isoformat())

# Get the value - factory is automatically invoked
timestamp = container.get("timestamp")
print(timestamp)  # "2024-01-01T12:00:00.000000"

docs.title: With Dependencies
docs.text:
class Database:
    def query(self, sql: str) -> list:
        return [{"id": 1, "name": "Alice"}]

class Cache:
    def get(self, key: str) -> Any:
        return None

# Factory that depends on Database and Cache
def create_user_service(db: Database, cache: Cache) -> UserService:
    """Factory with DI - parameters resolved automatically."""
    return UserService(db, cache)

container.bind(Database, Database).singleton()
container.bind(Cache, Cache).singleton()
container.bind_factory(UserService, create_user_service)

# Dependencies are automatically injected
service = container.get(UserService)

docs.title: Parameterized Factories (Manual Arguments)
docs.text: When you need to pass custom arguments to a factory function at call time, use parameterized factories.

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ

container = InjectQ()

# Data store
data = {
    "user:1": {"name": "Alice", "age": 30},
    "user:2": {"name": "Bob", "age": 25},
    "user:3": {"name": "Charlie", "age": 35},
}

# Bind a parameterized factory
container.bind_factory("data_store", lambda key: data.get(key))

# Method 1: Get factory then call
factory = container.get_factory("data_store")
user1 = factory("user:1")
print(user1)  # {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}

# Method 2: Use call_factory shorthand
user2 = container.call_factory("data_store", "user:2")
print(user2)  # {"name": "Bob", "age": 25}

# Method 3: Chain the calls
user3 = container.get_factory("data_store")("user:3")
print(user3)  # {"name": "Charlie", "age": 35}

docs.title: Multiple Parameters
docs.text:
def calculator(operation: str, a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Factory that performs calculations."""
    operations = {
        "add": a + b,
        "subtract": a - b,
        "multiply": a * b,
        "divide": a / b if b != 0 else 0,
    }
    return operations.get(operation, 0)

container.bind_factory("calculator", calculator)

# Use with different operations
result_add = container.call_factory("calculator", "add", 10, 5)
result_multiply = container.call_factory("calculator", "multiply", 10, 5)

print(f"10 + 5 = {result_add}")      # 15
print(f"10 * 5 = {result_multiply}") # 50

docs.title: Keyword Arguments
docs.text:
def create_config(env: str = "dev", debug: bool = False, port: int = 8000) -> dict:
    """Factory that creates configuration objects."""
    return {
        "environment": env,
        "debug": debug,
        "port": port,
        "url": f"http://localhost:{port}",
    }

container.bind_factory("config", create_config)

# Call with different configurations
dev_config = container.call_factory("config", env="dev", debug=True)
prod_config = container.call_factory("config", env="prod", debug=False, port=80)

print(dev_config)   # {"environment": "dev", "debug": True, ...}
print(prod_config)  # {"environment": "prod", "debug": False, ...}

docs.title: get_factory(service_type)
docs.text:
Returns the raw factory function without invoking it.

Signature: 

def get_factory(self, service_type: ServiceKey) -> ServiceFactory:
    """Get the raw factory function without invoking it."""

Parameters: - service_type: The service type or key for the factory

Returns: - The factory function

Raises: - DependencyNotFoundError: If no factory is registered

Example: 

container.bind_factory("data_store", lambda key: data[key])

# Get the factory function
factory = container.get_factory("data_store")

# Call it with your own arguments
result = factory("key1")

docs.title: call_factory(service_type, *args, **kwargs)
docs.text:
Convenience method that gets and calls a factory in one step.

Signature: 

def call_factory(self, service_type: ServiceKey, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
    """Get and call a factory function with custom arguments."""

Parameters: - service_type: The service type or key for the factory - *args: Positional arguments to pass to the factory - **kwargs: Keyword arguments to pass to the factory

Returns: - The result of calling the factory function

Raises: - DependencyNotFoundError: If no factory is registered

Example: 

container.bind_factory("calculator", lambda op, a, b: operations[op](a, b))

# Call with arguments directly
result = container.call_factory("calculator", "add", 10, 5)

docs.title: 1. Data Access Patterns
docs.text:
# Repository pattern with dynamic queries
class UserRepository:
    def __init__(self, db: Database):
        self.db = db

    def find_by_id(self, user_id: int):
        return self.db.query(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_id}")

container.bind(Database, Database).singleton()

# Bind as parameterized factory
container.bind_factory(
    "user_repo_query",
    lambda user_id: container.get(UserRepository).find_by_id(user_id)
)

# Use it
user = container.call_factory("user_repo_query", 123)

docs.title: 2. Configuration Management
docs.text:
# Environment-specific configurations
def create_db_config(env: str, pool_size: int = 10):
    configs = {
        "dev": {"host": "localhost", "port": 5432, "db": "dev_db"},
        "prod": {"host": "prod-db.example.com", "port": 5432, "db": "prod_db"},
    }
    config = configs.get(env, configs["dev"])
    config["pool_size"] = pool_size
    return config

container.bind_factory("db_config", create_db_config)

# Get different configs
dev_config = container.call_factory("db_config", "dev")
prod_config = container.call_factory("db_config", "prod", pool_size=50)

docs.title: 3. Connection Pooling
docs.text:
class ConnectionPool:
    def __init__(self, db_name: str, max_connections: int = 10):
        self.db_name = db_name
        self.max_connections = max_connections

container.bind_factory(
    "db_pool",
    lambda db_name, max_conn=10: ConnectionPool(db_name, max_conn)
)

# Create different pools for different databases
users_pool = container.call_factory("db_pool", "users_db", max_conn=20)
orders_pool = container.call_factory("db_pool", "orders_db", max_conn=15)

docs.title: 4. Dynamic Service Creation
docs.text:
# Service factory that creates services based on type
def create_notification_service(channel: str):
    services = {
        "email": EmailNotificationService(),
        "sms": SMSNotificationService(),
        "push": PushNotificationService(),
    }
    return services.get(channel)

container.bind_factory("notification", create_notification_service)

# Get different notification channels
email_service = container.call_factory("notification", "email")
sms_service = container.call_factory("notification", "sms")

docs.title: ✅ Do's
docs.text:
1. Use DI factories for services with dependencies 

    # Good - dependencies auto-injected
container.bind_factory(UserService, lambda db, cache: UserService(db, cache))
service = container.get(UserService)

  2. Use parameterized factories for dynamic data access 

    # Good - allows custom parameters
container.bind_factory("get_user", lambda user_id: fetch_user(user_id))
user = container.call_factory("get_user", 123)

  3. Combine both patterns when needed 

    # DI factory
container.bind_factory("logger", lambda: create_logger())
logger = container.get("logger")

# Parameterized factory
container.bind_factory("data", lambda key: data[key])
value = container.call_factory("data", "key1")

  4. Use descriptive factory names 

    # Good
container.bind_factory("get_user_by_id", lambda id: ...)
container.bind_factory("create_db_connection", lambda db_name: ...)

# Bad
container.bind_factory("factory1", lambda x: ...)
container.bind_factory("f", lambda a, b: ...)

docs.title: ❌ Don'ts
docs.text:
1. Don't use get() for parameterized factories 

    # Bad - will fail with DI resolution
container.bind_factory("data", lambda key: data[key])
value = container.get("data")  # ERROR: 'key' not found

# Good
value = container.call_factory("data", "key1")

  2. Don't mix DI and manual parameters in the same factory 

    # Confusing - some params from DI, others from caller
def mixed_factory(db: Database, user_id: int):
    return db.get_user(user_id)

# Better - separate concerns
def di_factory(db: Database) -> UserRepository:
    return UserRepository(db)

container.bind_factory("user_repo", di_factory)
repo = container.get("user_repo")
user = repo.get(123)  # Separate the parameter passing

  3. Don't overuse parameterized factories 

    # Bad - too many parameters
container.bind_factory("create_everything", 
    lambda a, b, c, d, e, f, g: ...)

# Good - use a class or split into smaller factories
class ConfigBuilder:
    def build(self, a, b, c, d, e, f, g):
        ...

container.bind(ConfigBuilder, ConfigBuilder).singleton()

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text: Feature DI Factories Parameterized Factories Binding bind_factory("service", factory) bind_factory("service", factory) Resolution get("service") call_factory("service", args) Parameters Auto-resolved from container Passed by caller Use Case Services with dependencies Dynamic data access Caching Respects scope (singleton, transient) Always transient Example User service with DB/cache deps Get user by ID

docs.title: Migration Guide
docs.text:
If you have existing code that tries to use parameterized factories with get():

Before: 

# This doesn't work
container.bind_factory("data", lambda key: data[key])
value = container.get("data")  # ERROR

After: 

# Use get_factory or call_factory
container.bind_factory("data", lambda key: data[key])

# Option 1: Get factory then call
factory = container.get_factory("data")
value = factory("key1")

# Option 2: Use shorthand
value = container.call_factory("data", "key1")
