docs.title: FastAPI Integration
docs.text:
setup_fastapi adds one middleware to your app. InjectFastAPI is a dependency marker for routes.

pip install injectq[fastapi]

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import FastAPI
from injectq import InjectQ
from injectq.integrations.fastapi import InjectFastAPI, setup_fastapi


class UserService:
    def get_user(self, user_id: int) -> dict:
        return {"id": user_id, "name": "John Doe"}


container = InjectQ()
container.bind(UserService, UserService)

app = FastAPI()
setup_fastapi(container, app)


@app.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user(
    user_id: int,
    service: Annotated[UserService, InjectFastAPI(UserService)],
) -> dict:
    return service.get_user(user_id)

docs.title: What setup_fastapi(container, app) does
docs.text:
It stores the container on app.state and adds InjectQRequestMiddleware, a pure ASGI middleware. For every HTTP request and WebSocket connection it:

  1. makes container the current container (a ContextVar),
  2. enters container.async_scope("request"),
  3. runs the app,
  4. closes the scope, so request-scoped resources are torn down, and restores the previous container.

So:

  • @scoped services and @resource("request") resources live for one request (one WebSocket connection for WebSockets).
  • Inside a route, InjectQ.get_instance() and @inject use the container you passed to setup_fastapi, not the global one.
  • Sync routes run in worker threads that copy the context, so they see the same container and scope.
  • Other requests and other apps never see this container.

Call setup_fastapi once. Do not also add InjectQRequestMiddleware yourself.

docs.title: InjectFastAPI(ServiceType)
docs.text:
A FastAPI Depends that resolves the service with await container.aget(...), so async factories are awaited. It works in HTTP routes and WebSocket handlers, sync and async.

@app.get("/report")
async def report(
    repo: Annotated[ReportRepo, InjectFastAPI(ReportRepo)],
    ctx: Annotated[RequestContext, InjectFastAPI(RequestContext)],
) -> dict:
    return {"request_id": ctx.request_id, "rows": repo.count()}

Without setup_fastapi, resolving raises InjectionError ("No InjectQ container in the current FastAPI request context").

docs.title: Request scope
docs.text:
from uuid import uuid4

class RequestContext:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.request_id = str(uuid4())


container.bind(RequestContext, RequestContext, scope="request")

@scoped on the class does the same for the global container (bare @scoped means "request").

Two dependencies on RequestContext in the same request get the same object. The next request gets a new one. Resolving a request-scoped service outside a request (at import time, in a startup hook) raises ScopeError; use with container.scope("request"): there.

If a route raises, the scope closes with that exception, and request-scoped resources see it in their teardown. Your own exceptions reach FastAPI unchanged.

docs.title: get_container_fastapi(connection=None)
docs.text:
Returns the current context container, or else the one stored on the app (found through connection: a Request, WebSocket or ASGI scope). Raises InjectionError if there is none.

from fastapi import Request
from injectq.integrations.fastapi import get_container_fastapi


@app.get("/debug")
def debug(request: Request) -> dict:
    return {"services": len(get_container_fastapi(request).get_dependency_graph())}

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Build the app with a test container and use TestClient. To replace one service in an app that is already wired, use container.override. Requests made through TestClient inside the block see it.

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient


def test_get_user():
    with container.override(UserService, FakeUserService()):
        with TestClient(app) as client:
            assert client.get("/users/1").json()["name"] == "Test User"

Note

InjectAPI is the deprecated name of InjectFastAPI. See the migration guide.

Next: FastMCP, Taskiq.

docs.title: FastMCP Integration
docs.text:
setup_fastmcp adds one middleware to a FastMCP server. InjectFastMCP is a dependency marker for tools, resources and prompts.

pip install injectq[fastmcp]     # needs fastmcp>=2.14.0

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from fastmcp import FastMCP
from injectq import InjectQ
from injectq.integrations.fastmcp import InjectFastMCP, setup_fastmcp


class UserService:
    def get_user(self, user_id: str) -> dict:
        return {"id": user_id, "name": "Ada"}


container = InjectQ()
container.bind(UserService, UserService)

mcp = FastMCP("UserServer")
setup_fastmcp(container, mcp)


@mcp.tool
def get_user(
    user_id: str,
    service: UserService = InjectFastMCP(UserService),
) -> dict:
    return service.get_user(user_id)

docs.title: What setup_fastmcp(container, mcp) does
docs.text:
It stores the container on the server and registers InjectQMCPMiddleware with mcp.add_middleware(...). For every MCP message (tool call, resource read, prompt, listing) the middleware:

  1. makes container the current container,
  2. enters container.async_scope("request") around the rest of the chain,
  3. closes the scope when the message is done, which runs @resource("request") teardowns.

So @scoped services live for one message, and inside a handler InjectQ.get_instance() and @inject use this container, not the global one.

Call setup_fastmcp once. Do not also pass InjectQMCPMiddleware to FastMCP(middleware=[...]): the middleware would run twice. Use that form instead of setup_fastmcp only when you need to control middleware order, and then the server has no stored-container fallback.

docs.title: InjectFastMCP(ServiceType)
docs.text:
A FastMCP dependency marker. FastMCP calls it when it builds the handler arguments, and it resolves with await container.aget(...), so async factories are awaited. FastMCP hides dependency parameters from the MCP schema, so clients only see user_id in the example above.

It works the same in tools, resources and prompts:

import json


@mcp.resource("data://status")
def status(service: UserService = InjectFastMCP(UserService)) -> str:
    return json.dumps(service.get_user("status"))


@mcp.prompt
def explain(topic: str, service: UserService = InjectFastMCP(UserService)) -> str:
    return f"Explain {topic} for {service.get_user('x')['name']}."

docs.title: Request scope
docs.text:
class CallContext:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.calls = 0


container.bind(CallContext, CallContext, scope="request")


@mcp.tool
def count(ctx: CallContext = InjectFastMCP(CallContext)) -> int:
    ctx.calls += 1
    return ctx.calls    # always 1: a new CallContext for every message

@scoped on the class does the same for the global container. Resolving a request-scoped service outside a message raises ScopeError.

docs.title: get_container_fastmcp()
docs.text:
Returns the current context container, or else the one stored on the active server. Raises InjectionError if there is none. Use it in helper functions; in handler signatures use InjectFastMCP.

from injectq.integrations.fastmcp import get_container_fastmcp


def current_user_service() -> UserService:
    return get_container_fastmcp().get(UserService)

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Build the server with a test container, or use container.override on the real one. With FastMCP's in-memory client:

from fastmcp import Client


async def test_get_user():
    with container.override(UserService, FakeUserService()):
        async with Client(mcp) as client:
            result = await client.call_tool("get_user", {"user_id": "1"})
    assert result.data["name"] == "Test User"

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No InjectQ container in the current FastMCP request context: setup_fastmcp(container, mcp) was not called on the server that runs the handler.
  • The FastMCP integration (fastmcp>=2.14.0) requires the 'fastmcp' package: install injectq[fastmcp].

Note

InjectMCP, setup_mcp and get_container_mcp are the deprecated names. See the migration guide.

docs.title: Taskiq Integration
docs.text:
setup_taskiq adds a middleware to a Taskiq broker. InjectTaskiq is a dependency marker for tasks.

pip install injectq[taskiq]

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from typing import Annotated

from injectq import InjectQ
from injectq.integrations.taskiq import InjectTaskiq, setup_taskiq
from taskiq import InMemoryBroker


class EmailService:
    def send_email(self, to: str, subject: str) -> None:
        print(f"Sending email to {to}: {subject}")


container = InjectQ()
container.bind(EmailService, EmailService)

broker = InMemoryBroker()
setup_taskiq(container, broker)


@broker.task
async def send_welcome_email(
    user_email: str,
    service: Annotated[EmailService, InjectTaskiq(EmailService)],
) -> None:
    service.send_email(user_email, "Welcome!")


async def main() -> None:
    task = await send_welcome_email.kiq("user@example.com")
    await task.wait_result()

docs.title: What setup_taskiq(container, broker) does
docs.text:
It stores the container on broker.state and adds InjectQTaskiqMiddleware. For every task the worker runs:

  1. pre_execute makes container the current container and enters a "request" scope.
  2. Taskiq resolves the task's InjectTaskiq(...) parameters with await container.aget(...), so async factories are awaited.
  3. The task runs. In an async def task, InjectQ.get_instance() and @inject use container.
  4. post_execute (or on_error) closes the scope and restores the previous container. @resource("request") teardowns run here and see the task's exception if it failed. An error while closing the scope is logged, not raised, so Taskiq can still save the task result.

Each task gets its own request scope, so @scoped services are new for every task:

class TaskContext:
    pass


container.bind(TaskContext, TaskContext, scope="request")   # or @scoped on the global container

Sync tasks

On a worker, Taskiq runs a plain def task with loop.run_in_executor, which does not copy the context. Inside the body of a sync task, InjectQ.get_instance() and @inject do not see the broker's container. InjectTaskiq(...) parameters still work because they are resolved before the body runs. Use them, or make the task async def.

docs.title: InjectTaskiq(ServiceType)
docs.text:
A TaskiqDepends marker. Use it with Annotated:

@broker.task
async def process_order(
    order_id: int,
    orders: Annotated[OrderService, InjectTaskiq(OrderService)],
) -> dict:
    return orders.process(order_id)

docs.title: get_container_taskiq(state=None)
docs.text: Returns the current context container, or else the one stored on state (the broker's TaskiqState). Raises InjectionError if there is none.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Use InMemoryBroker with a test container, and read results through wait_result():

import pytest
from injectq import InjectQ


class FakeEmailService:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.sent: list[str] = []

    def send_email(self, to: str, subject: str) -> None:
        self.sent.append(to)


@pytest.fixture
def email() -> FakeEmailService:
    return FakeEmailService()


@pytest.fixture
def broker(email):
    container = InjectQ()
    container.bind(EmailService, email)       # an instance is bound as is
    broker = InMemoryBroker()
    setup_taskiq(container, broker)
    return broker


async def test_welcome(broker, email):
    @broker.task
    async def welcome(
        to: str,
        service: Annotated[EmailService, InjectTaskiq(EmailService)],
    ) -> None:
        service.send_email(to, "Welcome")

    result = await (await welcome.kiq("a@example.com")).wait_result()
    assert not result.is_err
    assert email.sent == ["a@example.com"]

To replace one service on a container that is already wired, use container.override.

Note

InjectTask and get_injector_instance_taskiq are the deprecated names. See the migration guide.

docs.title: Modules and Providers
docs.text:
A module groups related bindings so you can install them together. Install a module with container.install_module(...) or pass a list when you create the container: InjectQ([DatabaseModule()]).

from injectq import InjectQ
from injectq.modules import Module

class DatabaseModule(Module):
    def configure(self, binder):
        binder.bind(Database, PostgresDatabase)
        binder.bind(UserRepository, UserRepositoryImpl)

container = InjectQ.get_instance()
container.install_module(DatabaseModule())

repo = container[UserRepository]

binder has bind(...), bind_instance(...) and bind_factory(..., scope=...). They take the same arguments as the container's methods. bind defaults to the singleton scope and bind_factory to transient.

docs.title: SimpleModule
docs.text:
A fluent list of bindings:

from injectq.modules import SimpleModule

module = (
    SimpleModule()
    .bind(Database, PostgresDatabase)
    .bind(Cache, RedisCache)
    .bind_instance("api_key", "secret-123")
)
container.install_module(module)

docs.title: ConfigurationModule
docs.text:
Binds each key of a dict to its value:

from injectq.modules import ConfigurationModule

container.install_module(ConfigurationModule({"db_host": "localhost", "db_port": 5432}))

host = container["db_host"]

docs.title: ProviderModule
docs.text:
Mark methods with @provider. The return annotation says what the method provides, and its parameters are injected like a constructor's.

from injectq.modules import ProviderModule, provider

class AppModule(ProviderModule):
    @provider(scope="singleton")
    def provide_database(self, config: DatabaseConfig) -> Database:
        db = Database(config)
        db.connect()
        return db

    @provider
    def provide_user_service(self, db: Database, logger: Logger) -> UserService:
        return UserService(db=db, logger=logger)

container.bind_instance("db_host", "localhost")
container.install_module(AppModule())

service = container[UserService]

Rules:

  • The return annotation is required. Without it, installing the module raises BindingError.
  • A bare @provider is transient: the method runs on every resolve. Use @provider(scope="singleton"), or any other scope name, when the service should be shared or when creating it has side effects such as connecting.

  • Providers can be async def. Resolve them with aget():

    @provider(scope="singleton")
async def provide_client(self) -> Client:
    return await Client.connect()

client = await container.aget(Client)

  • Parameters are matched in this order: an Inject[...] default, a bound key with the parameter's name, then the annotation. So db_host: str above is filled by bind_instance("db_host", ...).

  • Providers are found by scanning the class dictionaries and are installed in definition order. Properties are not evaluated. An error inside a provider is raised, not hidden.

  • Module state is available through self, so a module can take constructor arguments:

    class EnvironmentModule(ProviderModule):
    def __init__(self, environment: str):
        self.environment = environment

    @provider(scope="singleton")
    def provide_database_config(self) -> DatabaseConfig:
        if self.environment == "production":
            return DatabaseConfig(host="prod-db.example.com", ssl=True)
        return DatabaseConfig(host="localhost", ssl=False)

container.install_module(EnvironmentModule("production"))

docs.title: Organising modules
docs.text:
Keep one module per area (DatabaseModule, UserModule, EmailModule) instead of one large module. Install them all on the same container:

container = InjectQ([InfrastructureModule(), UserModule(), OrderModule()])

A later registration of the same key replaces an earlier one, so you can install a fake module after the real one in a test:

class FakeServicesModule(ProviderModule):
    @provider(scope="singleton")
    def provide_database(self) -> Database:
        return InMemoryDatabase()

def test_user_service():
    container = InjectQ([InfrastructureModule(), FakeServicesModule()])
    service = container[UserService]

For overrides inside one block, see Overrides.

Next: FastAPI integration | Testing

docs.title: Resources and Cleanup
docs.text: A resource is a service that needs cleanup, such as a connection to close or a file to flush. InjectQ runs the cleanup when its scope exits or when the container shuts down.

docs.title: @resource
docs.text:
Write a generator. Code before yield sets the resource up, code after yield tears it down. The container binds the resource under the type in the return annotation.

from collections.abc import Iterator
from injectq import InjectQ, resource

container = InjectQ()
container.activate()


class Pool: ...


@resource                       # singleton: created once
def pool() -> Iterator[Pool]:
    p = Pool()
    print("pool open")
    try:
        yield p
    finally:
        print("pool closed")


container[Pool]                 # prints "pool open"
container.shutdown()            # prints "pool closed"

Iterator[Pool], Generator[Pool, ...], AsyncIterator[Pool] and ContextManager[Pool] all bind Pool. Without a return annotation, the function itself is the key.

Async resources use async def with yield:

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator


@resource
async def client() -> AsyncIterator[HttpClient]:
    async with HttpClient() as c:
        yield c

# later
http = await container.aget(HttpClient)
await container.ashutdown()

Resolve async resources with aget(). get() raises InjectionError for a key that needs an async factory.

docs.title: Resources with a scope
docs.text:
@resource("request") creates the resource once per "request" scope and tears it down when the scope exits:

class Session: ...


@resource("request")
def session() -> Iterator[Session]:
    s = Session()
    try:
        yield s
    finally:
        print("session closed")


with container.scope("request"):
    s = container[Session]       # opened here
# "session closed" is printed here

Async resources need aget() and async_scope, because the teardown must be awaited:

async with container.async_scope("request"):
    s = await container.aget(AsyncSession)

A transient resource makes no sense (nobody would close it), so @resource("transient") raises ResourceError when the function is decorated.

docs.title: What teardown code sees
docs.text:
• If the scope block raises, the exception is passed to the resource. A generator resource gets it at the yield:

    @resource("request")
def tx() -> Iterator[Transaction]:
    t = Transaction()
    try:
        yield t
    except Exception:
        t.rollback()
        raise                # re-raise: the scope never swallows the error
    else:
        t.commit()

  • The exception always continues after teardown. A scope exit cannot suppress it.

  • Teardowns run last-created first.
  • If a teardown fails, the others still run. The failures are then raised together as an ExceptionGroup (Python 3.11+). On Python 3.10 you get the first error with the others in __notes__.

docs.title: Your own cleanup: exit stacks
docs.text:
Every active scope has an exit stack. Push a context manager or a callback onto it, and it runs when the scope exits, together with the resources:

with container.scope("request"):
    stack = container.current_exit_stack("request")
    stack.callback(print, "first pushed")
    stack.callback(print, "second pushed")
# prints "second pushed", then "first pushed"

In an async_scope the stack is an AsyncExitStack, so you can push async context managers with await stack.enter_async_context(...).

current_exit_stack(name) raises ScopeError if that scope is not active.

docs.title: Shutting down the container
docs.text:
Singleton resources live until you shut the container down:

container.shutdown()             # sync resources
await container.ashutdown()      # sync and async resources
  • Resources close in reverse order of creation.
  • Each closed resource is removed from the singleton cache. Resolving it again creates a new one.
  • Pass an exception to hand it to the teardown code: container.shutdown(exc).
  • shutdown() skips async resources. Use ashutdown() when you have any.
  • Teardown failures are collected and raised together, as described above.

Call it when the app stops, for example in a finally block. In FastAPI, call await container.ashutdown() from the lifespan handler:

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    yield
    await container.ashutdown()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

A resource is created once, even if many tasks or threads ask for it at the same moment. Two resources with the same function name in different modules do not replace each other.

docs.title: Resources not bound to a container
docs.text:
get_resource_manager() gives access to the global resource manager. get_resource_manager().shutdown_all() and await ...shutdown_all_async() close every initialised resource of every container. Prefer container.shutdown().

managed_resource(factory, cleanup) and async_managed_resource(factory, cleanup) are small context managers for ad-hoc use:

from injectq import managed_resource

with managed_resource(open_file, cleanup=lambda f: f.close()) as f:
    ...

docs.title: Scoped Services
docs.text:
A scoped service has one instance per scope block. Inside the block you get the same instance every time. A new block gives a new instance. For the scope basics, see Understanding scopes.

import uuid
from injectq import InjectQ, scoped

container = InjectQ()
container.activate()          # the decorator binds into the current container

@scoped("request")            # bare @scoped means "request" too
class RequestContext:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())

with container.scope("request"):
    ctx1 = container[RequestContext]
    assert ctx1 is container[RequestContext]

with container.scope("request"):
    assert container[RequestContext] is not ctx1

Without the decorator:

container.bind(RequestContext, RequestContext, scope="request")
container.bind_factory(DbSession, open_session, scope="request")

docs.title: Outside a scope
docs.text:
container[RequestContext]
# ScopeError: No active 'request' scope; enter one with container.scope('request')

This keeps a request-scoped object from leaking into the next request. Enter a scope, or use a framework integration that does it for you.

docs.title: Sync and async
docs.text:
with container.scope("request"):
    ctx = container[RequestContext]

async with container.async_scope("request"):
    ctx = await container.aget(RequestContext)

get() and aget() return the same instance inside one block. Use async_scope when your services need async teardown (Resources).

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
"request" and "action" exist by default. Other names need container.register_scope(name). The name in the with must match the name on the service:

@scoped("request")
class Service: ...

container.register_scope("session")
with container.scope("session"):
    container[Service]       # ScopeError: No active 'request' scope

docs.title: Nesting
docs.text:
Blocks of the same name can nest. Leaving the inner block restores the outer one:

with container.scope("request"):
    outer = container[RequestContext]
    with container.scope("request"):
        assert container[RequestContext] is not outer
    assert container[RequestContext] is outer

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
The active scope is stored in a ContextVar.

  • Tasks started inside a block (asyncio.create_task) see the block's instances.
  • asyncio.to_thread inside a block gets the caller's instances.
  • loop.run_in_executor and plain threading.Thread do not see the scope. Resolving a scoped key there raises ScopeError.
  • Two requests handled at the same time each have their own block.

See Context and concurrency.

docs.title: Web frameworks
docs.text:
You do not enter scopes yourself in a web app. The integration enters one "request" scope per HTTP request or WebSocket connection (FastAPI), per MCP message (FastMCP), or per task (Taskiq).

from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI
from injectq import InjectQ, scoped
from injectq.integrations.fastapi import InjectFastAPI, setup_fastapi

container = InjectQ()
container.activate()
app = FastAPI()
setup_fastapi(container, app)

@scoped
class UserContext:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.user_id: int | None = None

@app.get("/user/{user_id}")
def get_user(user_id: int, ctx: Annotated[UserContext, InjectFastAPI(UserContext)]):
    ctx.user_id = user_id          # this instance belongs to this request only
    return {"user_id": ctx.user_id}

docs.title: Clearing a scope
docs.text: container.clear_scope("request") drops the instances of the active scope, and container.clear_all_scopes() drops all of them. Neither runs teardown code. Leave the with block for that. You rarely need these.

docs.title: A singleton cannot depend on a scoped service
docs.text:
A singleton lives for the whole process, so it keeps the instance from the first request. Resolve the scoped service inside the request instead.

Next: Resources and cleanup | Singleton | Transient

docs.title: Singleton Scope
docs.text:
One instance per container, created on first use and reused after that. This is the default scope for bind, container[Key] = Class, @singleton and @register_as.

from injectq import InjectQ, singleton

container = InjectQ.get_instance()

@singleton
class Database:
    def __init__(self):
        print("Database created")

db1 = container[Database]   # prints "Database created"
db2 = container[Database]   # no output
assert db1 is db2

docs.title: Ways to bind
docs.text:
container.bind(Database, Database)                       # default scope is singleton
container[Database] = Database                           # dict style
container.bind_instance("config", AppConfig())           # a ready-made object
container.bind_factory(Pool, make_pool, scope="singleton")  # built by a factory, once

Dependencies are injected as usual. A singleton can depend on other singletons. It should not depend on a scoped service: it would keep the first request's instance. See Scoped services.

Re-binding a key drops that key's cached instance, so the next get builds a new one.

docs.title: Thread safety
docs.text:
Each singleton is created once, even when many threads or tasks ask for it at the same moment. get() and aget() return the same object. The object is shared, so its own mutable state must be safe for concurrent use:

@singleton
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def increment(self):
        with self._lock:
            self.count += 1

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
A singleton that needs teardown should be a @resource. container.shutdown() or await container.ashutdown() closes it.

Next: Transient | Scoped services

docs.title: Transient Scope
docs.text:
A new instance on every resolve. Nothing is shared or cached.

from injectq import InjectQ, transient

container = InjectQ.get_instance()

@transient
class EmailValidator:
    def validate(self, email: str) -> bool:
        return "@" in email

v1 = container[EmailValidator]
v2 = container[EmailValidator]
assert v1 is not v2

Without the decorator:

container.bind(EmailValidator, EmailValidator, scope="transient")
container.bind_factory(Report, make_report)      # factories are transient by default

A transient is rebuilt for each service that depends on it too, so two services that both depend on it get different instances.

docs.title: Use it for
docs.text:
Stateless helpers, validators, commands, and any object that should not share state. Because nothing is shared, a transient needs no locking.

Do not use it for things that are expensive to build or must be shared (connections, caches). Make those singletons and inject them into the transient:

@singleton
class Schema:
    def __init__(self):
        self.tables = load_schema()      # once

@transient
class Processor:
    def __init__(self, schema: Schema):
        self.schema = schema             # shared

Keep state in self, set in __init__. A class attribute such as count = 0 is shared by all instances.

A transient cannot own a resource: @resource("transient") raises ResourceError, because nothing would close it.

Next: Scoped services | Singleton

docs.title: Understanding Scopes
docs.text:
A scope decides how long a service instance lives and who shares it.

Scope Instances Use for singleton One per container, created on first use Database pools, config, caches transient A new one on every resolve Stateless helpers, validators request One per with container.scope("request") block Per-request state, sessions, unit of work action Works like request, under its own name A second, independent unit of work

You can also register your own scope names.

docs.title: Choosing a scope
docs.text:
from injectq import InjectQ, singleton, transient, scoped

container = InjectQ.get_instance()

@singleton
class Database: ...

@transient
class Validator: ...

@scoped("request")          # bare @scoped means "request"
class UserSession: ...

Without a decorator, pass the scope to bind. bind defaults to singleton:

container.bind(Database, Database, scope="singleton")
container.bind(UserSession, UserSession, scope="request")
container.bind_factory(Validator, make_validator)                    # transient by default
container.bind_factory(Session, make_session, scope="request")

Details: Singleton, Transient, Scoped services, Resources and cleanup.

docs.title: Entering a scope
docs.text:
with container.scope("request"):
    a = container[UserSession]
    assert a is container[UserSession]       # same block, same instance

with container.scope("request"):
    assert container[UserSession] is not a   # new block, new instance

async with container.async_scope("request"):
    session = await container.aget(UserSession)

container[UserSession]   # ScopeError: No active 'request' scope

Use async_scope when scoped services need async teardown. Resolving a scoped key outside a block raises ScopeError.

Frameworks enter a "request" scope for you: once per HTTP request (FastAPI), MCP message (FastMCP) or task (Taskiq).

docs.title: Custom scopes
docs.text:
container.register_scope("job")

@scoped("job")
class JobContext: ...

with container.scope("job"):
    ctx = container[JobContext]

Entering a name that is not request, action or registered raises ScopeError: Unknown scope. Registering "singleton" also raises ScopeError.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: When a block exits, its exit stack runs, last pushed first. @resource("request") services are closed there. See Resources and cleanup.

docs.title: Scopes and concurrency
docs.text: A scope lives in a ContextVar. Tasks and asyncio.to_thread calls started inside a block see it. run_in_executor and plain threads do not. Scopes belong to one container: two containers never share instances. See Context and concurrency.

docs.title: Picking wrongly
docs.text:
A singleton lives for the whole process, so request data in a singleton is shared by every request. A singleton that depends on a scoped service keeps the instance from the first request. Use scoped("request") for per-request state, and keep expensive objects (connections, parsed schemas) in singletons.

@singleton
class UserContext:       # wrong: one user_id for every request
    user_id = None

@scoped("request")
class UserContext:       # right: one per request
    user_id = None

Singletons are shared by all threads and tasks, so they must be safe to share. See Singleton.

docs.title: Overrides for Testing
docs.text:
container.override(key, value) swaps one dependency for the length of a with block. Use it to replace a database, a mailer or a clock in a test without touching your bindings.

from injectq import InjectQ


class Mailer:
    def send(self, to: str) -> str:
        return f"real mail to {to}"


class FakeMailer(Mailer):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.sent: list[str] = []

    def send(self, to: str) -> str:
        self.sent.append(to)
        return "fake"


class Notifier:
    def __init__(self, mailer: Mailer) -> None:
        self.mailer = mailer


class Api:
    def __init__(self, notifier: Notifier) -> None:
        self.notifier = notifier


container = InjectQ()
container.bind(Mailer, Mailer)
container.bind(Notifier, Notifier)
container.bind(Api, Api)

fake = FakeMailer()
with container.override(Mailer, fake):
    api = container.get(Api)
    assert api.notifier.mailer is fake       # Api -> Notifier -> Mailer

assert type(container.get(Api).notifier.mailer) is Mailer   # back to normal

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Transitive. Services that depend on the key, directly or through other services, get the override.
  • The value is returned as is. InjectQ does not copy, wrap or call it. Pass the object you want.
  • Nothing is registered. Bindings and cached singletons are left alone. After the block the key resolves exactly as before. Services that depend on the key are rebuilt inside the block, and those instances are cached for the block only.
  • Context-local. The override is visible to the current task or thread, and to tasks and to_thread calls started inside the block. Another test, request or thread running at the same time does not see it.
  • Works on every kind of key. Class bindings, instances, factory-bound keys and string keys. It also works when the container was created with allow_override=False. An override is not a re-binding.
  • Nests. Inner blocks win. Leaving an inner block restores the outer override.
container.bind_factory("clock", lambda: "real")

with container.override("clock", "frozen"):
    assert container.get("clock") == "frozen"
assert container.get("clock") == "real"

In 0.5, override() ignored factory-bound keys, cleared every singleton on entry and exit, and changed the container for all threads. See the migration guide.

docs.title: override_dependency
docs.text:
injectq.testing.override_dependency is the same thing as a function. It defaults to the global container:

from injectq.testing import override_dependency

with override_dependency(Mailer, fake, container=container):
    ...

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
The override layer lives in a ContextVar.

import asyncio

async def main():
    with container.override(Mailer, fake):
        inside = container.get(Mailer)                       # fake
        child = await asyncio.create_task(read(container))   # fake: tasks copy the context
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        pool = await loop.run_in_executor(None, container.get, Mailer)   # real Mailer
        thread = await asyncio.to_thread(container.get, Mailer)          # fake: to_thread copies it

run_in_executor and threading.Thread do not copy the context, so they see the real binding. See Context and concurrency.

For a clean container per test instead of a swap, see isolated_container and container_fixture.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• While any override is active, the container resolves through slower guarded resolvers. The fast paths return when the last override exits.
  • An override does not change objects that already hold the old value. A Notifier singleton built before the block keeps the real Mailer, and the same instance is returned after the block. Inside the block, container.get(Notifier) builds a new Notifier with the fake.

Next: Testing patterns

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Three tools cover most tests:

Tool Use it to isolated_container() get a fresh container that is also the global and current container for the block container.override(key, value) replace one dependency for a block, context-local and transitive MockModule bind mocks and fixed values as a module

docs.title: isolated_container()
docs.text:
from injectq.testing import isolated_container


def test_user_service():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container[Database] = MockDatabase()
        container[UserService] = UserService

        service = container[UserService]
        assert service.get_user(1) is not None

The container becomes the global instance (InjectQ.get_instance()) and the current context container, so @inject and the registration decorators (@singleton, @scoped, ...) use it too. Both are restored when the block ends.

docs.title: container_fixture(name="container")
docs.text:
Creates a pytest fixture that yields an isolated_container(). Assign it to a module-level name in conftest.py:

# conftest.py
from injectq.testing import container_fixture

container = container_fixture()                 # fixture named "container"
other = container_fixture(name="other")         # fixture named "other"

def test_notifier(container):
    container.bind(Mailer, FakeMailer)
    ...

docs.title: Overriding one dependency
docs.text:
def test_with_fake_mailer(container):
    container.bind(Mailer, Mailer)
    container.bind(Notifier, Notifier)

    with container.override(Mailer, FakeMailer()):
        assert isinstance(container.get(Notifier).mailer, FakeMailer)

injectq.testing.override_dependency(key, value, container=None) is the same call as a function, defaulting to the global container. See Overrides for the rules.

docs.title: Other helpers
docs.text:
• MockModule().mock(Type, **attrs).bind_value(key, value) builds a module of instance bindings. See Testing patterns.
  • mock_factory.create_mock(Type, **attrs) returns a simple mock whose other methods return "mock_<name>_result".
  • create_test_module({Key: value, ...}) builds a MockModule from a dict.

Note

test_container, TestModule and pytest_container_fixture are the deprecated names of isolated_container, MockModule and container_fixture. See the migration guide.

Next: Testing patterns.

docs.title: Unit test with mocks
docs.text:
Bind the doubles, let the container build the real service.

from injectq.testing import isolated_container


class MockUserRepository:
    def __init__(self):
        self.users = {}
        self.save_called = False

    def save(self, user):
        self.save_called = True
        self.users[user.id] = user
        return user


def test_create_user():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        repo = MockUserRepository()
        container[UserRepository] = repo
        container[UserService] = UserService

        user = container[UserService].create_user("john@example.com")

        assert user.email == "john@example.com"
        assert repo.save_called

Mock the edges (APIs, databases, email) and use real internal services.

docs.title: Mock modules
docs.text:
MockModule binds mocks and fixed values as instances:

from injectq import InjectQ
from injectq.testing import MockModule

module = (
    MockModule()
    .mock(EmailService, sent=[])          # attributes become fields on the mock
    .bind_value("db_url", "sqlite://")
)
container = InjectQ(modules=[module])

The mock returned by .mock(...) answers any other method call with "mock_<name>_result". For checks on arguments, write your own double or use unittest.mock.

docs.title: Factories
docs.text:
Factories bound with bind_factory can be called with your own arguments through call_factory:

def test_parameterized_factory():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container.bind_factory("pool", lambda db, max_conn=10: Pool(db, max_conn))

        pool = container.call_factory("pool", "users_db", max_conn=20)

        assert (pool.db, pool.max_conn) == ("users_db", 20)

To replace a factory-bound key in a test, use container.override("pool", fake_pool).

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
A request scope is one with block. Resolving outside it raises ScopeError:

import pytest
from injectq import ScopeError


def test_request_scope():
    with isolated_container() as container:
        container.bind(RequestData, RequestData, scope="request")

        with container.scope("request"):
            assert container[RequestData] is container[RequestData]

        with pytest.raises(ScopeError):
            container[RequestData]

For async code use async with container.async_scope("request"):.

docs.title: Overrides in tests
docs.text:
Override one dependency and everything that depends on it sees the fake:

def test_notifier_uses_fake(container):
    container.bind(Mailer, Mailer)
    container.bind(Notifier, Notifier)

    fake = FakeMailer()
    with container.override(Mailer, fake):
        container.get(Notifier).notify("a@example.com")

    assert fake.sent == ["a@example.com"]

docs.title: Avoiding shared state
docs.text: Tests that call InjectQ.get_instance() and bind into it leak bindings into other tests. Use isolated_container() or the container_fixture() fixture instead, or override for a single swap.
